item.title: Seth's Blog: The Hallmark dilemma
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/the-hallmark-dilemma/

The slogan is “when you care enough to send the very best.”

But more accurately, it’s “when you don’t care enough to be on the hook.”

For a low-stakes social interaction, the Hallmark card is a convenient and safe solution. Low-risk, it gets the job done. People don’t blame you for letting someone from Kansas say a nice thing on your behalf.

Now, it’s happening at scale. If you want to be left off the hook, AI is a convenient excuse. Do what it says. Ask it what to dress up as for this Halloween, or what to write in your marketing copy. Let it design your website or write your resume. Perhaps you could have it write your wedding vows as well.

Our culture prizes convenience ahead of just about everything else, and AI slop is convenient. It saves us time but it also saves us emotional labor.

The dilemma is obvious. Unlike a Hallmark card, AI is available to do just about everything. And when we’ve streamlined our life to a convenient nub of its former self, then what?

There’s a different path. Insist that AI ask you questions. Challenge it to challenge you.

Then choose. Sign your work.

AI isn’t the cause of slop, and it’s not a good excuse for slop either.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The pass-through of retail crime
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/the-pass-through-of-retail-crime.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=the-pass-through-of-retail-crime

This paper shows retailers increase prices in response to organized retail crime. We match store-level crime data to scanner data from the universe of transactions for cannabis retailers in Washington state. Using quasi-experimental variation from robberies and burglaries, we find a 1.7–1.8 percent price increase at victimized stores and nearby competitors. This rise is not driven by short-to-medium-term demand changes but is consistent with crime-related cost shocks. Effects are larger for independent stores and less concentrated markets. We estimate crime imposes a 1 percent “hidden” unit tax on affected stores, implying $30.7 million in additional social costs, primarily borne by consumers.

That is from a newly published paper, AEJ: Economic Policy, by Carl Hase and Johannes Kasinger.

The post The pass-through of retail crime appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Doomberg: Gating Functions
item.description:
Original article: https://newsletter.doomberg.com/p/gating-functions

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history. To the victor belong the spoils, right?” – Donald J. Trump

In the late summer of 2021, heavy oil production in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt temporarily crashed by 25%. The proximate cause of the decline was the need to divert lighter grades of domestically produced crude to the country’s struggling refineries. Those lighter hydrocarbons would normally have been used as diluents to enable transporting Orinoco’s otherwise solid-like oil sludges to markets near and far. Absent the lights, production of the heavies had to be curtailed.

Black goo | Bloomberg

The root cause of the mini-crisis was the cumulative effect of years of suffocating sanctions levied against Venezuela by successive US administrations that made external sourcing of materials, capital goods, and investor money progressively more difficult. In the final weeks of 2025, such financial weapons were supplemented with floating ones, as the US Navy imposed a partial blockade of oil tankers into and out of the beleaguered country. Among those inbound, a few that of Russian origin found themselves in a particularly interesting showdown:

“A tanker subject to US sanctions carrying some 300,000 barrels of naphtha from Russia entered Venezuelan waters late on Thursday, while another began redirecting course in the Atlantic Ocean, ship tracking data showed, a reflection of diverging last-minute decisions by ship owners after President Donald Trump ordered a ‘blockade’ of oil tankers under sanctions bound for the OPEC country earlier this week.

The move ramped up pressure on Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro by targeting the country’s main source of income and followed the seizure by the US of an oil tanker off the coast of Venezuela earlier in December.”

The naphtha en route from Russia was itself meant to serve as diluent, and Venezuela’s inability to source it in sufficient quantities was once again contributing to precipitously falling production. The escalating pressure campaign that followed culminated in the US Army’s elite Delta Force successfully snatching President Nicolás Maduro in early January, a jarring inflection point in the long-standing geopolitical skirmish between the two countries.

Heavy stuff | Getty

Maduro’s abrupt departure left behind a government that was more pliant to US President Donald Trump’s demands. Much of the sanctions pressure exited with the former strongman, and the flow of diluent in and heavy crude out rebounded markedly. According to a recent report delivered to acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez last week, oil production reached a remarkable 1.25 million barrels per day (bpd)—up from a low of just 830,000 bpd in December—due to higher production in the Orinoco Belt and conventional crude production gains.

If one closely examines the political and molecular mayhem that has so characterized the Venezuelan oil industry over the past decade, powerful evidence emerges for many of the core themes regularly argued in these pages. Included among them are proof of the shifting molecular definition of oil itself, a proper ranking of politics ahead of geology in the hierarchy of constraints on oil production, and—perhaps most importantly—a window into the true hydrocarbon potential of the Western Hemisphere. Let’s head to Caracas to explore each in order.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Being a light
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/31/being-a-light/

I’ve played a lot of pickup soccer over the years, with plenty of players who were genuinely good. Not Messi good. Pickup good.

Within that group there’s a tier of players who have the full trifecta: ball control, game intelligence, and communication. The ball seems to stick to their feet, and they always seem to have more time on it than everyone else.

But even within that tier, only a few rise to being great.

The difference is what they do with their skills. Great players lift the team up. They give feedback, they push the bar higher, but they do it as a light, not as a judge.

The skilled ones, who often have the exact same technical attributes, tend to make life harder for everyone around them, not because their instruction is wrong, but because of how they deliver it.

I see the same pattern at work. People who seem unhurried, who always find the right pass, whose communication shows up as much in how they act as in what they say.

It’s a beautiful thing to watch and to aspire to.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The unintended consequences of academic leniency
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/the-unintended-consequences-of-academic-leniency.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=the-unintended-consequences-of-academic-leniency

Education is widely recognized as the primary driver of human capital accumulation. However, policies designed to promote educational attainment often overlook students’ endogenous responses. This paper provides empirical evidence of the causal impact of relaxed academic standards on student effort and achievement. We find that academic leniency results in mechanical GPA increases, but significant reductions in effort among lower ability students based on lower attendance and lower numerical grades. These heterogeneous effects compound and exacerbate gaps in engagement and achievement throughout high school, ultimately worsening deficits in human capital accumulation as measured by ACT scores.

That is from a newly published paper, in AEJ: Economic Policy, by A. Brooks Bowden, Viviana Rodriguez, and Zach Weingarten.

The post The unintended consequences of academic leniency appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

“He who lives to see two or three generations is like a man who sits some time in the conjurer’s booth at a fair, and witnesses the performance twice or thrice in succession. The tricks were meant to be seen only once; and when they are no longer a novelty and cease to deceive, their effect is gone.” — Schopenhauer

item.title: Seth's Blog: Cooperation (the fall book list)
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/cooperation-the-fall-book-list/

Last week’s book list was a success, and I realized that it would work even better with others. Bookstores work precisely because they stack the books right next to each other.

Even though each of these authors has a book out this fall, they’re not my competition. Too often, we avoid cooperation because we’re embracing scarcity.

Each of us will be linking to thehotlist.org today. Ideas that spread, win. The page automatically updates based on which books get clicked on the most.

What happens when you help connect and organize the others?

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Better Incentives, More Kidneys, More Lives
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/better-incentives-more-kidneys-more-lives.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=better-incentives-more-kidneys-more-lives

The organ procurement system has long been a miasma of inefficient monopoly providers. In 2024 I quoted some shocking facts from a great Statecraft interview with Jennifer Erickson and Greg Segal:

“Organs are literally lost and damaged in transit every single week. The OPTN contractor is 15 times more likely to lose or damage an organ in transit than an airline is a suitcase.”

Organs are not GPS-tracked!

“In an era when consumers can precisely monitor a FedEx package or a DoorDash dinner delivery, there are no requirements to track shipments of organs in real time — or to assess how many may be damaged or lost in transit.

“If Amazon can figure out when your paper towels and your dog food is going to arrive within 20 to 30 minutes, it certainly should be reasonable that we ought to track lifesaving organs, which are in chronic shortage,” Axelrod said.

Here’s one more astounding statistics:

“Seventeen percent of kidneys are offered to at least one deceased person before they are transplanted….”

Did you get that? The tracking system for patients is so dysfunctional that 17% of kidneys are offered to patients who are already dead–thus creating delays and missed opportunities.

Fortunately, even then there were changes in the works. In 2019 President Trump issued Executive Order 13879 to improve the performance of OPOs with better incentives and to allow living donors to recover more of their costs. The government being what it is, it has taken years to implement some of the new rules and enforcement of the OPO performance measures was deferred to 2026-2027. Nevertheless, there have been improvements. For example, many OPOs now GPS-track kidney transfers. And a new report estimates there have been significant gains from the changes.

The Advancing American Kidney Health initiative was launched by President Donald Trump via Executive Order 13879 on July 10, 2019. In this Data Point, we estimate the range of increased growth in transplants that might be attributed to the policies launched through the Executive order and the economic value of that increased growth.

The estimated impacts of the Executive Order (EO) range from a conservative 1,055 additional transplants annually to an upper estimate of 2,110 additional transplants. The range reflects variation in the counterfactuals used to compare with post-2019 transplant growth.

Under the conservative-case scenario, the policy is estimated to be associated with approximately 23,214 additional kidney transplants between 2019 and 2040, generating about 147,410 life-years gained and 21,821 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained. Under the optimistic-case scenario, the policy is estimated to be associated with approximately 46,428 additional kidney transplants between 2019 and 2040, generating about 294,819 life-years gained and 43,643 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) gained.

The biggest and most consequential change would be to allow payment to living organ donors. The End Kidney Deaths Act, H.R. 2687, proposes a $50,000 refundable tax credit over five years for qualifying nondirected living kidney donors. The act has bipartisan support. Because dialysis is so expensive—and the federal government pays for much of it through Medicare’s special kidney-failure entitlement—the Act could save taxpayers money as well as saving lives.

Hat tip: The indefatigable Elaine Perlman.

The post Better Incentives, More Kidneys, More Lives appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Are there too many misdemeanor convictions?
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/are-there-too-many-misdemeanor-convictions.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=are-there-too-many-misdemeanor-convictions

Maybe so:

Misdemeanors account for three-quarters of criminal cases filed annually in the United States, yet causal evidence on the impacts of misdemeanor conviction is scarce. We combine administrative and survey data to provide novel evidence of how misdemeanor conviction affects the socioeconomic outcomes of defendants and their families. Using data on nearly seven million defendants from 11 states, we characterize the types of people involved with the misdemeanor system. We estimate causal impacts of a conviction relative to a charge using seven county reforms that sharply reduced conviction rates. Regression discontinuity design estimates yield precise null average effects of the reforms on criminal and labor market outcomes. Defendants dismissed by the reform are unlikely to re-offend if dismissed, but also unlikely to be harmed by conviction—marginal defendants are older and more likely to have been charged with minor crimes than the average defendant. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that conviction harms young and first-time defendants, implying that interventions targeting dismissal toward these groups would be beneficial. Finally, our causal estimates imply a negative Marginal Value of Public Funds of misdemeanor conviction, even under plausible estimates of general deterrence effects.

That is from recent research by Nikhil Rao and James Reeves, note that Rao is this year on the job market from University of Michigan.

The post Are there too many misdemeanor convictions? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Three things that annoy me about myself right now
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/30/three-things-that-annoy-me-about-myself-right-now/

I took some time recently to reflect on the three things I find most annoying about myself at the moment. It’s a useful exercise to revisit periodically. My current list is:

(1) Letting people finish their thought instead of letting excitement or impatience get the better of me. This is a long-term project. It’s the dark side of a strength: a bias for action. The balance is tricky, but I’ve made some recent progress in my own self-awareness around it, and that gives me hope.

(2) Removing “like” and other filler words has been an on-and-off project for years, and it’s been consistently on my mind this past year. My awareness here isn’t consistent yet, and that’s usually the first step.

(3) Changing my relationship with my phone entirely. I wrote about this recently and my effort to simplify how I use the internet. I’m testing a few things and I’m excited about testing leaving the phone in one room of the house after work, so I get used to not having it on me. I’m hopeful it continues.

As with most things like this, noticing isn’t enough. I’ve made some commitments and added this to my weekly review. I’m hoping to be annoyed by different problems twelve months from now.

More to follow.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Chronicle of Higher Education interviews me on AI and education
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/chronicle-of-higher-education-interviews-me-on-ai-and-education.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=chronicle-of-higher-education-interviews-me-on-ai-and-education

Scott Carlson did the work (gated, but free with registration), here is one excerpt:

Cowen: …Another proposal I’ve made is that schools should let people do one class, only one class, AI-only — no professor, except a professor grades at the end. The professor grades not answers to an exam but the workflow of how the student used AI to learn the Glorious Revolution, or the Civil War, or whatever the student learned. Eventually, another AI will grade your AI log. But let’s start today with a professor, and try this for one class. I’m not sure how it will go. But especially for small schools that don’t offer that many classes, a student now can create a class in literally everything.

If it’s successful, let them try two classes. I think the students doing this on their own are more likely to figure out how to blend AI and education than we would from a distance with some kind of centralized vision. Let them experiment.

Carlson: Students should be leading the change at colleges and universities?

Cowen: Absolutely. Students know more about AI than their professors do. Some of this comes from cheating, which is unfortunate. But the notion that the professors teach the students AI — I wish. It’s not always possible. You could imagine setting up a class where the students teach the professors AI, and we give the students credit for teaching. I’m half joking, but it’s not, in fact, a crazy idea. We need to experiment along a number of fronts. I’m quite convinced no one knows how to do this. It hasn’t been done before. So again, just one class. In general, schools hate this idea. They see it as opening the door to rendering some professors obsolete.

And this:

Carlson: There are a number of students who are deeply opposed to AI. What place do they have in this university that you’re thinking about?

Cowen: I would love to have different schools with different policies. If some universities try to ban AI altogether, that’s great. Let the competitive process operate. Personally, I would bet against those schools. For a long time, I’ve been worried that within a given tier of school — big state school, community college, Ivy League — there’s not enough diversity. AI policies will force a kind of diversity on us. So I’m all for no-AI schools, even though I would not go to one.

Recommended.

The post Chronicle of Higher Education interviews me on AI and education appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: “Curious Address”
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/30/curious-address/

I send you a post-card which I received in the ordinary way by post from my brother, who lives at Sutton Scarsdale, a scattered village near Chesterfield. You will notice that the card was posted at 7.15 p.m. on the 5th October, and it was delivered during the evening of the following day. The address looks a mixture of Greek and German, but on inspection it will be found that each letter is spelled out in full. The pencilled words were inserted by the Post Office officials. The Post Office is often the object of complaints for tardiness in delivery, but I think great credit is due to it for its cleverness and promptness in this case. — Mr. John Alderson, 12, Albert Road, Stroud Green, N.

From the Strand, January 1904. I make out the text as:

Hemr. Jay Hayhelldeehearesohhen

12, Hayhellbehearetea Areohhaydee

Steaareohyoudee Geearehehehen

London N.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/can-artificial-intelligence-forecast-treatment-effects-in-economics.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=can-artificial-intelligence-forecast-treatment-effects-in-economics

I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects of research studies pre-registered on the AEA RCT Registry and the Open Science Framework. I focus on studies whose results were first publicly released in 2026 and elicit forecasts from models whose training or knowledge cut-off dates were before the relevant set of papers was released. First, LLM models extract forecasting questions from the pre-registrations or pre-analysis plans. These questions elicit forecasted treatment effects; not all resolve in the subsequent papers, but those that do can be used to consider forecast accuracy. Forecasts were elicited for 889 treatment effects from 39 papers with results disclosed in January 2026 or later, or 673 from 33 papers after screening. Forecasts were elicited in raw units but I focus on those that could be standardized and therefore compared across papers. Currently, the median absolute forecast error is 0.054 SD for the best model, the average absolute error is 0.093 SD, and the MSE is 0.0218. The AI forecasts perform substantially better than benchmarks forecasting 0 effect or forecasting the mean effect of other papers’ results in that time period. Overall, these results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to be of value in informing policy and research.

From the excellent Eva Vivalt. As I have been predicting, so much of economics (and science) is going to change, and radically. Here is Eva’s thread on the paper. Perhaps we should dispense with many of the more mundane inquiries, and as Eva notes: “But can we not shift to working on those projects that have particularly high uncertainty and upside potential?”

She is one of the best young economists in the world, and this stands some chance of being the most important paper of the year.

The post Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: Turnabout
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/29/turnabout-22/

An “enigma in praise of women,” from an 1820 miscellany:

Happy that man may pass his life,

Who’s free from matrimonial chains;

Who is directed by a wife,

Is sure to suffer for his pains.

What tongue is able to unfold

The falsehood which in women dwell?

The worth in women you behold

Is almost imperceptible.

Adam could find no solid peace

When Eve was given him for a mate;

Till he beheld a woman’s face,

Adam was in a happy state.

See, in the female race appear

Hypocrisy, deceit, and pride;

Truth, darling of a heart sincere,

In women never can reside.

They’re always studying to employ

Their time in malice and in lies;

Their leisure hours in virtuous joy

To spend, ne’er in their thoughts arise.

Destruction take the men, I say,

Who make the fair their chief delight;

Who no regard to women pay,

Keep reason always in their sight.

“By reading the first and third lines together the Enigma is explained.”

item.title: Marginal Revolution: How Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok Have Changed Their Views on AI and Where They Disagree (part 2 of 2)
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/how-tyler-cowen-and-alex-tabarrok-have-changed-their-views-on-ai.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-tyler-cowen-and-alex-tabarrok-have-changed-their-views-on-ai

From the Archives-written by ChatGPT.

Both became dramatically more confident in AI’s capabilities while remaining optimistic about its economic potential. Their differences concern how benefits arrive, how seriously to weight emerging dangers, and whether AI might possess consciousness. Cowen emphasizes institutions, bottlenecks, and geopolitical competition. Tabarrok emphasizes inexpensive intelligence, scientific discovery, and—especially in his later writing—concrete safety failures.

The dated passages below trace those changes across the public archive. Quotations are the authors’ own words, including excerpts from their columns; outside material they reproduce is identified separately.

Early views on unequal gains and abundance

Cowen’s early framework grew out of chess. On March 11, 2011, he observed that stronger computers required stronger human partners:

“The required education level — for the team’s ‘wage premium’ — is ratcheted up.”

His concern was already distributional: computers could increase productivity while changing which human skills commanded a premium. He also emphasized learning how to work with computers. What I learn from chess and computers.

Tabarrok’s April 12, 2016 argument was more explicitly reassuring:

“AI will be cheap and ownership will be widespread.”

He compared AI to an increase in the world’s supply of educated people: more intelligence produces useful ideas, and competition spreads the benefits to consumers. But his forecast of comprehensive substitution was cautious—AI becoming a perfect substitute for human intelligence could be “100 years or more” away. Will the proliferation of affordable AI decimate the middle class?

Neither position was absolute. Cowen warned in February 2017 that the Industrial Revolution involved decades of painful adjustment; historical progress did not guarantee quick wage gains. Tabarrok, in October 2019, praised the argument that mediocre automation could displace workers without creating enough additional wealth to compensate. See Cowen’s historical warning and Tabarrok’s Beware the Mediocre Robots!

Rising confidence in AI capabilities from 2020 to 2025

Cowen was already optimistic about language models in July 2020. After publishing a skeptical reader’s assessment of GPT-3, he added:

“I remain bullish, but it is always worth considering other opinions.”

That attribution matters: the skeptical arguments in the post were the reader’s, not Cowen’s. The case against the import of GPT-3, July 23, 2020.

Tabarrok’s shift toward near-term transformative AI became unmistakable by March 2, 2023:

“I never expected to witness the birth of aliens.”

Later that month, he endorsed Microsoft researchers’ description of GPT-4 as exhibiting an incomplete form of general intelligence: “They are correct.” This is a substantial acceleration from his 2016 outlook, although perfect substitution for humans and early general intelligence are different thresholds. See AGI is Coming and Baby AGI is Here, March 24, 2023.

Cowen reached an especially explicit formulation on April 16, 2025, discussing o3:

“I think it is AGI, seriously.”

But he immediately separated capability from adoption:

“It still will take us a long time to use it properly.”

His growing enthusiasm about the technology did not imply an equally dramatic forecast for immediate economic growth. o3 and AGI, is April 16th AGI day?

Economic transformation and the pace of adoption

On January 6, 2025, Tabarrok wrote:

“The intelligence revolution is going to be bigger, more impactful and more wrenching than the industrial revolution.”

This is his own concluding sentence, following a quotation from Sam Altman. The Intelligence Revolution.

Cowen’s February 23, 2025 response to rapid-takeoff expectations focused on a different constraint:

“Human bottlenecks become more important, the more productive is AI.”

Energy, regulation, organizational habits, and weak human collaborators can constrain the economic value of better models. He offered an explicitly tentative estimate of an additional half percentage point of annual growth—large when compounded, but far from an immediate economic explosion. Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow.

By September 3, 2026, Tabarrok was developing the distributional implications:

“A smaller share of a much larger economy can still mean more income for labor.”

He argued that even substantial displacement could leave aggregate labor income higher, or make compensation affordable. He explicitly acknowledged painful losses for particular workers. His high-growth calculations are scenarios, not forecasts. How Much Redistribution Will AI Require?

They also converge more than their rhetoric suggests. In May 2026, Cowen rejected mass unemployment while identifying transitional hiring problems. In August 2026, Tabarrok interpreted business-survey evidence as consistent with their shared position that AI had not yet broadly reduced employment. See Cowen, May 13, and Tabarrok, August 31.

Growing attention to safety and institutional limits

Cowen stated his central position on November 19, 2023:

“I view AI as more likely to lower than to raise net existential risks.”

His reasoning was comparative: the world already faces serious dangers, and stronger science could improve our defenses. My summary views on AI existential risk.

Tabarrok’s later writing places more weight on specific vulnerabilities. On April 8, 2026, he described:

“the worrying combination that very powerful AI’s are very vulnerable.”

He was discussing cybersecurity capabilities alongside agents’ susceptibility to manipulation. AI Risks.

On September 17, 2026, he sharpened the institutional objection to assuming that beneficial science will automatically offset dangerous capabilities:

“But faster science does not automatically mean faster defense.”

This can be read as a qualification of Cowen’s earlier optimism: defensive discoveries must pass through institutions that may move slowly. It also applies Cowen’s own bottleneck logic to safety. Pandemic Preparation is AI Safety.

Cowen nevertheless supports safeguards. In August 2026, he proposed government-overseen, industry-led safety audits. In September, he opposed restrictions on recursive improvement as impractical to enforce internationally. His position is therefore selective regulation combined with continued development. See his August 27 proposal and September 22 critique.

The September 2026 exchange about AI leaders

On September 16, 2026, Tabarrok rejected the claim that executives’ safety warnings were merely marketing or regulatory capture:

“Amodei actually believes what he’s saying.”

He did not thereby establish that the warnings or proposed policies were correct. His argument concerned sincerity and incentives. What Regulatory Capture Actually Looks Like.

Cowen replied the next day:

“I agree with Alex that the standard model of regulatory capture does not apply here”

But he emphasized competition for power: each executive sincerely thinks their own company should win. For Cowen, that complicates treating their warnings as disinterested policy advice. They agree that concern is sincere; they differ over which incentives best explain behavior. The correct model of AI CEO behavior, September 17, 2026.

Consciousness and Tabarrok’s warning about infant pain

On March 17, 2025, Tabarrok’s What Did We Learn From Torturing Babies? drew a moral lesson from medicine’s historical dismissal of infant pain. He described how theories about immature brains allowed physicians to discount babies’ observable distress and perform procedures without adequate anesthesia. His warning explicitly extended to judgments about animals and AI:

“If we must err, let us err on the side of compassion.”

Tabarrok’s position is stronger than mere openness to AI consciousness: he argues for moral caution under uncertainty. The analogy does not establish that AI suffers. It challenges confidence that a theory ruling out suffering is sufficient grounds to disregard possible evidence of it.

On October 14, 2025, he went further in his own commentary following an essay by Jack Clark:

“these systems are becoming self-aware”

He distinguished self-awareness from sentience, while warning against confidently dismissing the latter. His link accompanying that warning points back to the infant-pain essay, making the connection explicit. We Turned the Light On—and the AI Looked Back.

Cowen’s position is much more categorical. On August 31, 2026, he wrote:

“I am very much opposed to the view that the AIs are sentient, or might be sentient.”

He treats AI sentience as a category error, although he accepts that human-like descriptions can sometimes help predict AI behavior. Anthropomorphizing AI?

The disagreement concerns both what AI might experience and how to act when we cannot confidently know. Tabarrok’s historical analogy places greater weight on the moral cost of mistakenly denying consciousness; Cowen expresses much greater confidence that sentience is the wrong category to apply. These are their philosophical assessments, not established findings about AI consciousness.

The post How Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok Have Changed Their Views on AI and Where They Disagree appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Explaining funny
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/explaining-funny/

This is one of the most famous comedy bits of all time:

But why is it funny? The disconnect between experiencing it and explaining it represents one of the challenges of teaching. It’s also at the heart of leadership, marketing and culture.

Design, good taste, genre, communication style–these are all human endeavors that inform our days, but most of the time, we’re at a loss to explain them.

Abbott and Costello are avatars, approachable and relatable to their audience. You can see yourself as one or the other, depending on the moment. They’ve plotted an intricate dialogue, one that builds on itself, gaining traction and increasing tension as it goes. And as each expresses their frustration with the situation (and to a degree, with each other), it’s easy to put ourselves in their shoes.

We’ve never been in this exact situation, but we’ve all experienced a moment like this.

Most of us are in on the joke as we watch it. We know it’s a joke, and we understand early on the nature of the wordplay. So much so that the sketch itself becomes an icon, one that others are based on, sometimes with great fidelity:

Funny even before the reign of U2. So iconic that it’s now a three-word shorthand.

We can have the same discussion about your logo. Or why your book cover is less than it could be.

When someone is designing a bridge, we don’t have to wonder if the engineer “gets it.” The metrics are obvious and easily measured. We have precise words and numbers that are external to our own experience and the zeitgeist, and whether a person or a machine does the calculations, it works or it doesn’t.

But much of the rest of the human experience is often too layered and nuanced to be reduced to a simple formula. We need to notice enough and engage enough to get it. That’s what Heinlein was talking about when he coined the 60s term grok.

When a municipality sets aside the resources to build a ‘signature’ bridge, their own Golden Gate, there’s often a conflict. Not just disagreement about the need for something more than the utility of moving across the river, but also understanding what beautiful and important even looks like. Some people don’t get it.

Saying “that’s not funny,” or “I think it’s ugly,” is easy. The difficult work is acknowledging that someone else might disagree.

Human emotions require a viewer, not just a creator. The funny, the beauty, the elegance: they happen for someone, in their experience.

“That’s not beautiful,” is not the same as, “I don’t think that’s beautiful.”

I don’t have to explain a joke or a sculpture or a logo. But I do have to know enough to imagine that someone else is going to get it. We can choose to care enough to figure out why someone gets something we don’t, and imagine what it might take to create something human enough that others will care about it.

There’s no algorithm, which is part of the point.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: How Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok Have Changed Their Views on AI and Where They Disagree (part 1 of 2)
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/how-tyler-cowen-and-alex-tabarrok-have-changed-their-views-on-ai.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-tyler-cowen-and-alex-tabarrok-have-changed-their-views-on-ai

From the Archives-written by ChatGPT.

Both became dramatically more confident in AI’s capabilities while remaining optimistic about its economic potential. Their differences concern how benefits arrive, how seriously to weight emerging dangers, and whether AI might possess consciousness. Cowen emphasizes institutions, bottlenecks, and geopolitical competition. Tabarrok emphasizes inexpensive intelligence, scientific discovery, and—especially in his later writing—concrete safety failures.

The dated passages below trace those changes across the public archive. Quotations are the authors’ own words, including excerpts from their columns; outside material they reproduce is identified separately.

Early views on unequal gains and abundance

Cowen’s early framework grew out of chess. On March 11, 2011, he observed that stronger computers required stronger human partners:

“The required education level — for the team’s ‘wage premium’ — is ratcheted up.”

His concern was already distributional: computers could increase productivity while changing which human skills commanded a premium. He also emphasized learning how to work with computers. What I learn from chess and computers.

Tabarrok’s April 12, 2016 argument was more explicitly reassuring:

“AI will be cheap and ownership will be widespread.”

He compared AI to an increase in the world’s supply of educated people: more intelligence produces useful ideas, and competition spreads the benefits to consumers. But his forecast of comprehensive substitution was cautious—AI becoming a perfect substitute for human intelligence could be “100 years or more” away. Will the proliferation of affordable AI decimate the middle class?

Neither position was absolute. Cowen warned in February 2017 that the Industrial Revolution involved decades of painful adjustment; historical progress did not guarantee quick wage gains. Tabarrok, in October 2019, praised the argument that mediocre automation could displace workers without creating enough additional wealth to compensate. See Cowen’s historical warning and Tabarrok’s Beware the Mediocre Robots!

Rising confidence in AI capabilities from 2020 to 2025

Cowen was already optimistic about language models in July 2020. After publishing a skeptical reader’s assessment of GPT-3, he added:

“I remain bullish, but it is always worth considering other opinions.”

That attribution matters: the skeptical arguments in the post were the reader’s, not Cowen’s. The case against the import of GPT-3, July 23, 2020.

Tabarrok’s shift toward near-term transformative AI became unmistakable by March 2, 2023:

“I never expected to witness the birth of aliens.”

Later that month, he endorsed Microsoft researchers’ description of GPT-4 as exhibiting an incomplete form of general intelligence: “They are correct.” This is a substantial acceleration from his 2016 outlook, although perfect substitution for humans and early general intelligence are different thresholds. See AGI is Coming and Baby AGI is Here, March 24, 2023.

Cowen reached an especially explicit formulation on April 16, 2025, discussing o3:

“I think it is AGI, seriously.”

But he immediately separated capability from adoption:

“It still will take us a long time to use it properly.”

His growing enthusiasm about the technology did not imply an equally dramatic forecast for immediate economic growth. o3 and AGI, is April 16th AGI day?

Economic transformation and the pace of adoption

On January 6, 2025, Tabarrok wrote:

“The intelligence revolution is going to be bigger, more impactful and more wrenching than the industrial revolution.”

This is his own concluding sentence, following a quotation from Sam Altman. The Intelligence Revolution.

Cowen’s February 23, 2025 response to rapid-takeoff expectations focused on a different constraint:

“Human bottlenecks become more important, the more productive is AI.”

Energy, regulation, organizational habits, and weak human collaborators can constrain the economic value of better models. He offered an explicitly tentative estimate of an additional half percentage point of annual growth—large when compounded, but far from an immediate economic explosion. Why I think AI take-off is relatively slow.

By September 3, 2026, Tabarrok was developing the distributional implications:

“A smaller share of a much larger economy can still mean more income for labor.”

He argued that even substantial displacement could leave aggregate labor income higher, or make compensation affordable. He explicitly acknowledged painful losses for particular workers. His high-growth calculations are scenarios, not forecasts. How Much Redistribution Will AI Require?

They also converge more than their rhetoric suggests. In May 2026, Cowen rejected mass unemployment while identifying transitional hiring problems. In August 2026, Tabarrok interpreted business-survey evidence as consistent with their shared position that AI had not yet broadly reduced employment. See Cowen, May 13, and Tabarrok, August 31.

Growing attention to safety and institutional limits

Cowen stated his central position on November 19, 2023:

“I view AI as more likely to lower than to raise net existential risks.”

His reasoning was comparative: the world already faces serious dangers, and stronger science could improve our defenses. My summary views on AI existential risk.

Tabarrok’s later writing places more weight on specific vulnerabilities. On April 8, 2026, he described:

“the worrying combination that very powerful AI’s are very vulnerable.”

He was discussing cybersecurity capabilities alongside agents’ susceptibility to manipulation. AI Risks.

On September 17, 2026, he sharpened the institutional objection to assuming that beneficial science will automatically offset dangerous capabilities:

“But faster science does not automatically mean faster defense.”

This can be read as a qualification of Cowen’s earlier optimism: defensive discoveries must pass through institutions that may move slowly. It also applies Cowen’s own bottleneck logic to safety. Pandemic Preparation is AI Safety.

Cowen nevertheless supports safeguards. In August 2026, he proposed government-overseen, industry-led safety audits. In September, he opposed restrictions on recursive improvement as impractical to enforce internationally. His position is therefore selective regulation combined with continued development. See his August 27 proposal and September 22 critique.

The September 2026 exchange about AI leaders

On September 16, 2026, Tabarrok rejected the claim that executives’ safety warnings were merely marketing or regulatory capture:

“Amodei actually believes what he’s saying.”

He did not thereby establish that the warnings or proposed policies were correct. His argument concerned sincerity and incentives. What Regulatory Capture Actually Looks Like.

Cowen replied the next day:

“I agree with Alex that the standard model of regulatory capture does not apply here”

But he emphasized competition for power: each executive sincerely thinks their own company should win. For Cowen, that complicates treating their warnings as disinterested policy advice. They agree that concern is sincere; they differ over which incentives best explain behavior. The correct model of AI CEO behavior, September 17, 2026.

Consciousness and Tabarrok’s warning about infant pain

On March 17, 2025, Tabarrok’s What Did We Learn From Torturing Babies? drew a moral lesson from medicine’s historical dismissal of infant pain. He described how theories about immature brains allowed physicians to discount babies’ observable distress and perform procedures without adequate anesthesia. His warning explicitly extended to judgments about animals and AI:

“If we must err, let us err on the side of compassion.”

Tabarrok’s position is stronger than mere openness to AI consciousness: he argues for moral caution under uncertainty. The analogy does not establish that AI suffers. It challenges confidence that a theory ruling out suffering is sufficient grounds to disregard possible evidence of it.

On October 14, 2025, he went further in his own commentary following an essay by Jack Clark:

“these systems are becoming self-aware”

He distinguished self-awareness from sentience, while warning against confidently dismissing the latter. His link accompanying that warning points back to the infant-pain essay, making the connection explicit. We Turned the Light On—and the AI Looked Back.

Cowen’s position is much more categorical. On August 31, 2026, he wrote:

“I am very much opposed to the view that the AIs are sentient, or might be sentient.”

He treats AI sentience as a category error, although he accepts that human-like descriptions can sometimes help predict AI behavior. Anthropomorphizing AI?

The disagreement concerns both what AI might experience and how to act when we cannot confidently know. Tabarrok’s historical analogy places greater weight on the moral cost of mistakenly denying consciousness; Cowen expresses much greater confidence that sentience is the wrong category to apply. These are their philosophical assessments, not established findings about AI consciousness.

item.title: A Learning a Day: The invisible integration
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/29/the-invisible-integration/

I was using Ramp’s app for a work expense recently and realized I’d forgotten to upload the receipt, which normally kicks off an exceptions process.

Except the receipt was already there.

I asked how, and learned Ramp has a direct integration with Toast, the restaurant payment system. Pay with a Ramp card at a merchant on Toast, and the itemized receipt gets attached to your transaction automatically. No photo, no upload, nothing from you.

This is what good integrations do. They take manual load off the user without asking for anything in return.

It’s also one of the hardest things to prioritize when you’re building a product, because integrations like this rarely show up on a roadmap next to the flashier features competing for the same slot.

But the experiences that become invisible, because you made them that easy, are the ones users end up remembering most.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: AI dominates human peer reviews
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/ai-dominates-human-peer-reviews.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=ai-dominates-human-peer-reviews

We show that AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors. We then discuss how this result may inform journal policy choices, with concerning downsides as well as potential paths to increase publication speed and quality; reduce adversarial interactions; improve the experience of editors, reviewers, authors, and readers; and advance science.

By Gary King and Steven Worthington, not even using what are now the very best models, rather based on Claude Opus 4.8. The details of the dominance, as outlined in the paper, are striking. It is not close.

On my Saez and Zucman post, I find it striking that some people are complaining all of a sudden. Yet I have been offering, citing, and linking to commentary on published papers for twenty-four years now (and every single day). Sometimes it might just be a casual offhand remark from me, whether positive or negative. Typically this is simply taken in stride. It is when you pull out the bazookas, and offer oodles of high-powered analytics, more astute than human referees, and combined with the ability to pursue follow-up inquiries, that people start getting worried. Model that.

You can pick at individual criticisms from the AIs all you want, but the most damning observation is that the errors go in the ideological direction of the authors 97% of the time. That is exactly what (the human) Phil Magness said years ago, based on an extensive canvassing of their work. Basically we already knew that was true, and the AIs confirmed the human estimate.

On our side, we have taken steps, most of all the new MR archive, to make AI analysis of our work easier. Soon you will be able to read on MR what the AIs think are our worst posts, respectively (Alex has prepared this).

In the meantime, I encourage the NSF, prize committees, universities, tenure committees, journals, and so on to do as many of their own AI-enabled audits as possible. So far the world is not jumping at this opportunity. You can model that too.

The post AI dominates human peer reviews appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: My design Conversation with Roman Mars
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/my-design-conversation-with-roman-mars.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=my-design-conversation-with-roman-mars

Here is the audio, video, and transcript. Here is part of the episode summary:

Roman Mars has built one of podcasting’s great empires out of noticing things everyone else walks past. His show, 99% Invisible, has racked up over 500 million downloads telling stories about the unnoticed design choices that quietly shape how cities and objects work…

Tyler and Roman discuss street signs, why classic cars were so much more distinctive than today’s SUVs, Waymos, New Jersey jughandles, yellow streetlights, lane-stripe colors, why Houston keeps growing despite its lack of charm, whether any post-war American suburb is actually beautiful, the Chrysler Building’s rocky reception, brutalism done right and wrong, Central Park as an urban miracle, what Jane Jacobs got wrong, e-bike lanes, Tokyo’s bike-free transit model, the placelessness of global coffee shops, why the iPhone looks boring now, the ugliest country he’s visited, his love for Australia’s polymer notes, his soft spot for the dollar’s “locked in amber” weirdness, underground power lines, how to warn future civilizations about nuclear waste, why highway signs lie to you about speed limits, the principles of a great city flag, the Pocatello redesign saga, his own studio, why 99% Invisible works precisely because it’s audio-only, the most unusual habit behind his long productive career, and more.

Excerpt:

COWEN: Yes. One of my favorite topics, currency design. What’s your favorite currency in terms of how it looks?

MARS: Favorite? It’s like I love almost any of them with the US currency in dead last. I find things to love about them. I’ve done a story on Australian currency, which was one of the early polymer notes. I just like utility in currency. I like different sizes. I like different colors. I like the fact that they put on artists and people of note that are not founding fathers and presidents and stuff like this. I don’t know if I have a particular favorite, but I was entranced by the thoughtfulness and utility of Australian currency when I did a story about it. You could be blind and know what note you’re holding because of the size. They stand up pretty well, and they care about all kinds of things rather than just presidents and stuff.

COWEN: I loved Swiss currency pre-2021. They had Le Corbusier on, Giacometti, Honegger. In the 1980s, they had Euler on, the mathematician. Imagine putting Euler on your country’s currency.

MARS: That is a canvas that’s so available to us to represent more values than we have in the United States than just founding fathers and presidents and stuff. I think it’s just such a wasted opportunity.

COWEN: I like the dollar, though. I’m surprised you’re so negative. I like the weird esotericism: the eye, the pyramid. The design is bizarre. It announces to the world: “We’re crazy.”

MARS: There are things to love about it. I just think that its fussiness and filigree, we’re locked in, I think for important reasons, which is because the dollar is the most important currency in the world, to which all other currencies are pegged, and therefore you don’t change it lightly. You have to be very, very careful. It really locked it into amber in a way that is both beautiful to admire, but also really limits its utility as things move on, we get better things than linen-paper hybrids and especially different sizes and utility for people with different needs. I think that’s important. There’s definitely things to love about the dollar. The dollar has some charm.

COWEN: I like the arrogance of it also. A sense of we don’t need to make the denominations look so different. If you’re a foreigner, we expect you’ll come here a lot, you’ll master dollars. Maybe you use them in your home country as well. They don’t need to be different colors.

MARS: It is definitely a bold statement that you’re going to adapt to our way of being if you’re going to use the dollar, for sure.

Opinions throughout!

The post My design Conversation with Roman Mars appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: Zoology
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/29/zoology-3/

Description of the Lyon in Edward Topsell’s 1607 bestiary The History of Four-Footed Beasts:

Lyons bones have no marrow in them and are so hard that they will strike fire. Their neck is made of one stiffe bone, without any vertebras. They have five claws on the hinder feet and the balls of their eyes are black. Lyons eat but once in two days, and drink in like manner. Formerly in England a Lyon could tell noble blood from base. There is a variety of Lyon with human faces. As for the rest, the taile of a Lyon is very long, which they shake oftentimes, and by beating their sides therewith they provoke themselves to fight. The nether part of this taile is full of hairs and gristles, and some are of opinion that there is therein a little sting wherewithall the Lyon pricketh itselfe.

He adds, “I would not have the Reader … imagine I have … related all that is ever said of these Beasts, but only [what] is said by many.”

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Errors in the research of Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/errors-in-the-research-of-emmanuel-saez-and-gabriel-zucman.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=errors-in-the-research-of-emmanuel-saez-and-gabriel-zucman

AI issues its judgment:

138 papers audited

2,035 problems found

147 serious enough to change a headline number

69% of papers have at least one

97% of major and moderate errors with a clear direction overstate the paper’s claim

And on the method:

Two independent audits of each paper. One by Claude Opus 5.5, one by OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, neither seeing the other’s work. Each obtained the paper, its appendices and its replication data, recomputed the headline numbers from the authors’ own files and, where possible, from the original sources (tax statistics, national accounts, Federal Reserve and survey data), checked that cited sources say what is claimed, and probed every assumption the conclusions rest on.

Then an adjudicator. A third agent re-verified every claimed problem, tried to refute each one, discarded those that did not survive, searched for problems both auditors missed, and graded what remained by how far it undermines the paper’s own headline claim: major changes a core number materially, moderate affects secondary results or a core result modestly, minor is a presentation or arithmetic slip. Confidence is graded separately.

There is much, much more at the link, which goes through the research paper by paper, and with further sustained analyses behind the links. The survey is both extensive and thorough. (And I thank an anonymous MR reader for this work.)

I am not even sure what to say at this point. We need a radical revaluation of this work, and of the associated policy arguments. More generally, this is only a single step in the story of how AI is going to revise economic science, and indeed past research more generally. As I stress in many of my recent talks, there will be significant gains and losses in status, with the losses often outweighing the gains. I see this as one of those cases.

The post Errors in the research of Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: How is AI shaping economic research?
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/how-is-ai-shaping-economic-research.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-is-ai-shaping-economic-research

Does generative AI narrow or widen productivity gaps in research? We study the distributional effects of AI on research productivity in economics using evidence from three sources: NBER working-paper and publication records, text-based measures of LLM-assisted writing, and an original survey of 227 academic economists measuring AI use across research tasks. We first show that productivity gaps among NBER authors narrowed following ChatGPT’s release: authors without research assistants (RAs) published a larger share of papers in top-tier journals, while authors from smaller teams gained in working-paper output and publication speed. We then use the survey to examine how individual AI use affects research productivity. We find weak evidence that AI affects working-paper output on average, but there is substantial heterogeneity. Triple-difference estimates show that greater AI exposure narrows the output gap between researchers with and without RAs but widens the gap between senior and junior researchers. Selection into AI use follows a different pattern: junior researchers use AI more intensively and are more likely to use agentic tools. Thus, these differential productivity effects reflect differences in the returns to AI rather than selection into AI use. A model with diminishing returns to execution, increasing returns to conceptual capacity, and complementarity between the two explains how AI can alleviate disadvantages in research support while amplifying the returns to accumulated expertise. Over time, however, early convergence may give way to divergence as execution constraints recede and AI’s conceptual capabilities improve.

That is from Tianyu Jiang, who is this year a job market candidate from the University of Michigan. The paper is co-authored with Yuqing (Claire) Wang.

The post How is AI shaping economic research? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Inequality in Equal Land
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/inequality-in-equal-land.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=inequality-in-equal-land

Adam Nash has a good post on wealth inequality:

…Every year, we pull the most recent data from the US Census on household wealth, cut by age.

…invariably, the students’ initial response is a reaction to the apparent disparity in wealth between households based on age.

For many students, it just doesn’t seem fair at first blush. Households between the ages of 65 to 69 have a median net worth that is 9.83x that of households under 35. You can almost hear their cries, “the Baby Boomers are hoarding all the wealth!”

Almost all of the graph, however, is aging! Nash considers a totally equal society called Equal Land. In Equal Land:

Everyone works from the ages of 25 to 64, retiring at 65

Everyone lives to the age of 85

Everyone makes the same amount, $100,000 per year

Everyone saves 10% of their income, every year while they work

Everyone makes 8% on their savings, every year

Everyone spends 4% of their portfolio, every year in retirement

The result is that in equal land the distribution of wealth is even more unequal by age than in our world! This is not to say all or even most inequality is explained by age. Most inequality in our world is within-age, not between-age. But when you look at an age-wealth graph specifically, almost all of what you are seeing is just age and the power of compounding.

The post Inequality in Equal Land appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: Degree
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/28/degree/

Political controversies, as Mr. Graham Wallas has pointed out, ought to be conducted in quantitative terms. … The dispute between anarchism and bureaucracy at present tends to take the form of one side maintaining that we want no organization, while the other maintains that we want as much as possible. … Some people think that we keep our rooms too hot for health, others that we keep them too cold. If this were a political question, one party would maintain that the best temperature is the absolute zero, the other that it is the melting point of iron. Those who maintained any intermediate position would be abused as timorous time-servers, concealed agents of the other side, men who ruined the enthusiasm of a sacred cause by tepid appeals to mere reason. Any man who had the courage to say that our rooms ought to be neither very hot nor very cold would be abused by both parties, and probably shot in No Man’s Land. Possibly some day politics may become more rational, but so far there is not the faintest indication of a change in this direction.

— Bertrand Russell, Icarus, 1924

item.title: A Learning a Day: Things could always be worse
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/28/things-could-always-be-worse/

I heard someone recently describe a formative moment from his childhood. Every time something difficult happens to him now, he thinks back to what his mom said every time he told her something bad happened: “Oh honey, things could always be worse.”

He imitated her voice as he said it, and the whole group chuckled.

He said it’s the reason he’s an optimist today, because things could always be worse.

It isn’t a new idea. But hearing the story brought it to life in a beautiful way.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: AI hacking risks
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/ai-hacking-risks.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=ai-hacking-risks

That is the topic of my latest Free Press column (now there are gift links!), here is one excerpt, noting this is a worst-case scenario not a prediction:

Yet current systems are likely to prove more robust than that suggests. For one thing, they use a variety of different methods of protection, including public key cryptography, AES, and cryptographic hash functions, the latter not qualifying as encryption per se. While it is possible that all could fall at the same time, that seems unlikely.

The more likely scenario, assuming this comes to pass at all, is that public key encryption would become vulnerable first, but the American economy would shift toward the more secure forms of communication, most of all those that have secure cryptographic keys already established. We would also work harder to substitute into the “post-quantum” methods of encryption that are being developed and already are being used in browsers.

The transition would be very costly, but the end result would not be total insecurity. Furthermore, today’s major financial institutions already have invested in various backup systems, including offline security methods and alternative payment-processing channels. Smaller businesses would face more serious problems of transition, although they also would be lesser targets in the first place. As for you the individual, you might have to show up in person at your bank to make a major transaction, and that requirement, imposed collectively, would strain our systems to the utmost.

A second layer of protection is that the new math techniques likely would not be available to everyone. They might require technical sophistication and a willingness to break the law in some very serious ways and also risk hacking retaliation. In addition, many math breakthroughs simply shave down the safety margins on systems, rather than breaking them altogether, and in those cases the criminals still might need a lot of computing power at considerable expense.

That situation is hardly the same as a complete and sudden “open season” on all methods of cryptography. Furthermore, some of the wrongdoers in this position, even assuming they felt they could get away with their crimes, might prefer to siphon off money slowly, rather than bring down the entire financial system, which could hurt their own net wealth as well.

A further source of protection is that the math breakthroughs might come in stages, rather than all at once. For an example from another part of math, OpenAI has proven a quasi-Riemann hypothesis, and Terry Tao told me recently that this may open the door to solving the Riemann hypothesis proper. We now have advance notice that the Riemann hypothesis may be proven (or less likely, disproven). In similar fashion, intermediate advances may signal that cryptographic protections are vulnerable. We thus would have some time to adjust…

The most likely scenarios would play out in terms of probabilities, as people deal with risk before any large-scale hacking attack would come. Right now the chance of public key cryptography breaking down is on the radar screens of a relatively small number of people. Imagine that some advances in math occur, and the more sophisticated market participants start seeing something like a 10 percent chance that some forms of encryption might be vulnerable. Perhaps without much fanfare, some people would start selling their bitcoin, or they might wire their money to more secure banks, or perhaps they would hold more gold and short the market. Some hackers would invest more in the activity, including hacks without advanced AI, under the philosophy of “harvest now, decrypt later,” pulling in classified or confidential materials that previously were not worth capturing. Overall, it would be like the early days of Covid, when major bad news was pending but only a few individuals were acting on it. That state of affairs could persist for some period of time.

In any case it would not be good.

And this: “If you have thoughts on my latest column, or questions about AI or anything else, join me for an AMA (Ask Me Anything) this week on The Free Press Forum.

Paid subscribers can submit questions now. Not a subscriber? For a limited time, you can get 20% off at thefp.com/tyler.”

item.title: Futility Closet: Tic-Tac-Don’t
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/27/tic-tac-dont/

With best play on both sides, conventional tic-tac-toe (noughts and crosses) is always a draw. Played in three dimensions, though, in a 3×3×3 cube, it’s always a win for whichever player manages to take the central cell. In fact, a draw is impossible — there’s no way to fill the “board” with 14 crosses and 13 noughts without completing one or more winning paths.

What if we reverse the object so that the first player to complete such a path loses? Interestingly, in that case seizing the center cell is still the best strategy. Thereafter, whichever cell the second player chooses, the first player should take the cell diametrically opposite. Obviously this can’t create a winning triple that passes through the center, but neither can it create a triple that doesn’t pass through the center, because the second player would necessarily just have completed such a triple himself on the opposite side of the cube.

“So the first player cannot lose,” writes mathematician Solomon Golomb. “Thus, because no draws are possible on the 3×3×3 ‘board,’ he must win!”

(This is similar to the first player’s strategy in Henry Dudeney’s cigar puzzle.)

(Solomon W. Golomb, “Martin Gardner and Ticktacktoe,” in Erik D. Demaine, Martin L. Demaine, and Tom Rodgers, eds., A Lifetime of Puzzles, 2008.)

item.title: Seth's Blog: The half-life of disappointment
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/the-half-life-of-disappointment/

When things don’t turn out the way you pictured, how long does it take for you to move on?

Reducing this window of disappointment unlocks the path to creativity and leadership.

People who get over disappointment more quickly aren’t less excited about the project than the others. They realize that getting attached to an outcome doesn’t increase its likelihood, and in fact, makes it less likely that their next project will be as bold.

Turns out that this is a common practice among professionals in every field.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Eleven outstanding film and television reviews by Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/eleven-outstanding-film-and-television-reviews-by-tyler-cowen-and-alex-tabarrok.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=eleven-outstanding-film-and-television-reviews-by-tyler-cowen-and-alex-tabarrok

From the Archive–these posts are written by ChatGPT

These selections emphasize the quality of the criticism: original interpretations, close attention to the work, and arguments worth considering even when you disagree. They are not a ranking of the films and television shows themselves. The list includes five reviews by Tyler Cowen and six by Alex Tabarrok. Several of the original posts reveal major plot developments; the descriptions here keep those revelations to a minimum.

1. Tyler Cowen — The Devil Wears Prada: A Straussian Interpretation

July 2, 2006 · Film · Spoilers in the original review

“Make no mistake about it, this is a movie about sheer power lust.”

Cowen reads beneath the film’s apparent moral lesson about rejecting a demanding career. His interpretation asks which relationships the ending restores, whose approval still matters, and whether the heroine has actually escaped the ambitions she appears to renounce. The result is a compact argument about power, independence, and emulation. Why it belongs: A memorable example of Cowen’s ability to turn a popular entertainment into an argument about motives. Read it after watching, when you can assess his interpretation against the ending. Read Cowen’s original review

2. Alex Tabarrok — Fleabag and Killing Eve

June 6, 2019 · Television · Major spoilers

“Fleabag is much darker and more religious and mystical than most people realize.”

Tabarrok connects the two series through sexual power, moral agency, and religious failure. His reading of Fleabag draws on textual and visual parallels to argue that its comedy conceals a much darker moral structure. The comparison with Killing Eve expands the argument beyond a single protagonist. Why it belongs: One of his most ambitious pieces of television criticism. Its characterization is contestable, but the sustained interpretation gives readers something substantial to argue with. Read Tabarrok’s original review

3. Tyler Cowen — Toni Erdmann, Misunderstood Masterpiece

February 5, 2017 · Film · Major spoilers

“The emotionally unrewarding nature of contemporary cosmopolitan life, but also the limits of rootedness.”

Cowen brings together family relationships, corporate humiliation, gender, and the relationship between Germany and Eastern Europe. He resists treating the film as a simple celebration of authenticity against professional life. Both the cosmopolitan daughter and the father who disrupts her world become objects of scrutiny. Why it belongs: The review connects intimate discomfort to larger social structures without reducing the film to a single message. Cowen’s suggestion that some of the father’s appearances might be imaginary should be read as his speculative interpretation. Read Cowen’s original review

4. Alex Tabarrok — Perfect Days, in “What to Watch (or Not)”

August 7, 2025 · Film · Some spoilers

“the routine is also a narcotic for the lost.”

Tabarrok challenges the comforting interpretation of Perfect Days as a lesson in finding happiness through simple routines. He recognizes the beauty of the protagonist’s life while asking whether its carefully maintained rhythms also protect him from painful relationships. His discussion of “crown shyness” turns a natural image into a metaphor for emotional distance. Why it belongs: A concise, sensitive counterreading that allows beauty and avoidance to coexist. The film discussion appears within a composite post that also covers Ballard and Billy Joel. Read Tabarrok’s original review

5. Tyler Cowen — Her

December 29, 2013 · Film · Light spoilers

“Will they enslave us, will they be our dogs, our friends, our trading partners, or something else altogether?”

Cowen treats the film as an exploration of the possible relationships between humans and artificial intelligence. He also attends to its visual and literary ancestry, making the review more than a response to the premise. The central question is how unfamiliar forms of intelligence might fit into emotional and social life. Why it belongs: It captures intellectual excitement about a film while opening questions that extend far beyond it. Its 2013 date makes the discussion especially interesting to revisit amid later debates about AI companionship. Read Cowen’s original review

6. Alex Tabarrok — Contagion

September 19, 2011 · Film · Limited plot discussion

“we have been lucky not virtuous.”

Tabarrok uses the film to examine preparedness and the difficulty of taking rare but consequential risks seriously. The review’s force comes from the relationship between cinematic imagination and public attention: a movie can make a danger emotionally intelligible when abstract warnings fail. Why it belongs: A strong example of film criticism becoming an argument about institutions and risk perception. Read its scientific and preparedness claims in their historical context: this is a review written in 2011. Read Tabarrok’s original review

7. Tyler Cowen — Technology in Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey

June 17, 2018 · Film · Spoilers near the end

“Finally the Solow residual is explained!”

Cowen combines observations about technological forecasting with attention to cinematic form, musical pacing, and narrative risk. The economic joke is characteristic, but the review also makes a case for the film’s sensory power and for seeing it on a large screen. Why it belongs: An entertaining blend of economic thinking and aesthetic attention. It shows how a familiar classic can yield fresh observations when approached through several disciplines at once. Read Cowen’s original review

8. Alex Tabarrok — Daredevil and the Doctrine of Double Effect

November 25, 2018 · Television · Some season-three details

“As I thought about this more, however, the Thou Shall Not Kill trope is least objectionable in Daredevil.”

Tabarrok starts with an objection to the superhero convention against killing, then revises his judgment by considering Daredevil’s Catholic commitments. The interesting move is to assess the character’s choices within his own moral framework rather than only through the viewer’s preferred calculation of consequences. Why it belongs: Criticism that visibly changes its mind. The post offers a useful discussion of character consistency and moral reasoning; its account of theology is best treated as part of that argument rather than a comprehensive doctrinal explanation. Read Tabarrok’s original review

9. Tyler Cowen — Borgen Season Four

July 23, 2022 · Television · Thematic spoilers

“I wish the content had more of ‘my kind of liberalism,’ but maybe the right-wing cultural critique makes for better TV.”

Cowen considers political power, gender, Greenland, and the media while separating his political preferences from his judgment of the drama. He asks whether a critique he finds less congenial might nevertheless produce stronger television. Why it belongs: A particularly clear example of judging artistic achievement independently of ideological agreement. The post is most revealing as a reflection on what makes political drama work. Read Cowen’s original review

10. Alex Tabarrok — The Remarkable Life of Ibelin

January 16, 2025 · Documentary · Reveals the film’s central turn

“What defines an ideal romance? What constitutes true friendship?”

Tabarrok explores how the documentary changes our understanding of a disabled young man’s life through his online relationships. Its construction prompts questions about intimacy, embodiment, and the limits of what even close relatives can know about another person. Why it belongs: A humane review that uses the documentary’s form to reconsider the value of online life. Although the original post labels itself “No spoilers,” readers who want to experience the central revelation unprepared should watch first. Read Tabarrok’s original review

11. Alex Tabarrok — The Gaslighting of Parasite

June 25, 2020 · Film · Major spoilers

“the most willfully misinterpreted movie that I have ever seen.”

Tabarrok challenges the prevailing interpretation of Parasite as an indictment of economic inequality. He builds his counterreading around the families’ conduct, the poorer characters’ treatment of other workers, and recurring imagery of smell and contamination. He argues that the film’s moral judgments cut against the political expectations many critics bring to it. Why it belongs: One of his most provocative and sustained film interpretations, and an essential inclusion in this selection. His reading is contestable, especially his insistence that the film’s judgments are unambiguous. That tension makes it rewarding to discuss alongside Cowen’s The Devil Wears Prada review: both ask whether a film’s apparent message conceals a different account of power and ambition. Read Tabarrok’s original review

The post Eleven outstanding film and television reviews by Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
