item.title: Doomberg: Tough Comp
item.description:
Original article: https://newsletter.doomberg.com/p/tough-comp

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

“Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so.” – Galileo Galilei

Roughly two and a half years ago, we published “Mapping the War,” a guide to following the daily ebbs and flows of the war between NATO and Russia over Ukraine. In it, we listed several accessible open-source social media accounts that, despite their known biases, provided good signal in a sea of propagandistic noise.

One account profiled was the Military Summary channel on YouTube, an excellent source of real-time information that has collectively garnered more than 400 million views worldwide. By consuming the channel’s twice-daily, bite-sized summaries of the war, we became aware of several important developments long before they made headlines in the Financial Times or Washington Post. Among them were Ukraine’s huge assault on Russian cargo and tanker ships in the Sea of Azov in July, Russia’s retaliation by blockading Ukraine’s Black Sea ports and destroying Odesa’s port infrastructure, and countless other escalations.

Put your likes | Military Summary

One thing that stands out after watching hundreds of such episodes over the years is just how tough it is to inflict a knockout blow from the air using only long-range, standoff munitions. Consider Russia’s years-long campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Russia has fired thousands of highly advanced ballistic missiles and tens of thousands of cutting-edge drones in a seemingly relentless daily campaign, but only now, with Kyiv effectively out of air-defense missiles, is the target deteriorating at a truly alarming rate.

If you live in Britain, you have probably been told that this pace exists because Russia is a paper tiger whose missiles don’t shoot straight, or Russian President Vladimir Putin has cancer (did you see his hands twitch?), or his agents are too busy Q-Tipping your local politician’s bidet to focus on winning the war. In the rest of the world, the natural conclusion is that it is prohibitively difficult to inflict sufficient damage from afar to force capitulation, especially against a country as large and as clearly motivated to fight as Ukraine.

What a weirdo | The Telegraph

Against such a backdrop, breaking news published in the Wall Street Journal over the weekend piqued our interest:

“American warships in the Middle East are preparing for an escalation in fighting in case President Trump opts for a fresh round of attacks against Iran in the coming weeks, according to US officials familiar with the planning.

During a rare visit to a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer operating in the Arabian Sea, The Wall Street Journal observed flight operations, as well as a significant replenishment of munitions and supplies—including a large delivery of standoff land attack missiles and bunker-buster bombs designed to penetrate ground targets.”

Given Iran’s credible threats to unleash an extraordinarily violent response to any renewed strikes on its territory, just what, exactly, are US President Donald Trump and his advisers hoping to accomplish with yet another round of fighting? Is a civilization-ending knockout blow to Iran even remotely possible using a couple of aircraft carriers, some long-range bombers taking off stateside, and what remains of American air bases in the Middle East? Can we learn anything from how challenging it has been for Russia to deal such a blow to Ukraine, despite sharing a border more than 1,000 miles long and enjoying access to its entire formidable military-industrial complex for the task?

A direct comparison between Iran and Ukraine is not only readily available using open sources, but the numbers will come as a sobering shock. Let’s have a look.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Loyal to the absent
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/27/loyal-to-the-absent/

One ideal I’ve found hard to live up to: being consistently loyal to people who aren’t in the room. So much of what we talk about is our reaction to other people, because so much of our life is shaped by them.

Here’s an alternate ideal I’ve found helpful to aim for. With the people you work with regularly, or care about, be someone they know will tell them directly when there’s a problem. So, you never let things fester.

That way, when you do end up talking about them behind their back (and you likely will), the conversation stays focused on getting to the root of the problem.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Is “Who’s on First?” funny?
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/is-whos-on-first-funny.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=is-whos-on-first-funny

Well, no, it is not funny, it would be too easy to relieve the dramatic tension by having Abbott explain the actual situation to Costello. One is not wrong to call the whole thing stupid.

Yet there is another reading of the skit which stands at least some chance of being funny, though it is not funny either.

You will note that Louis Costello was an Italian-American and son of an immigrant, and he had the obvious class mannerisms of such a stereotype. Bud Abbott was half Jewish and I believe half some mainstream ethnicity. He is a stand-in for the establishment, part of which was Jewish and highly commercial. You can read the skit as a commentary on how the establishment rips off the “less tutored” immigrants and refuses to apologize for that or even to explain it. The establishment simply keeps on talking rings around the lower-class immigrant, whether or not those words make sense. The immigrant has no real recourse, as he is less articulate and is also less in control and can only play the role of boob. In essence, Abbott, by not telling Costello the real names of the players, is not letting the ethnic assimilate into that most American of pasttimes, namely baseball.

Note how Costello admits, early in the skit, that he is the one with the funny name (Sebastian Dinwitty in the skit, likely a take-off on “dimwit”). And Abbott, by speaking of the players as being named Who, What, and “I don’t know,” is expressing his frustration with an America that does not sound or look the same any more. Abbott is in essence saying “Hey, what is this? I was not expecting Ted Kluszewski in my country!” He is throwing the growing presence of immigrants in the country back in the face of the ethnic and then stonewalling it.

In the skit, Abbott has the name of “Mr. Broadhurst,” very reminiscent of the establishment.

The skit does show we had an America too obsessed with names, and to no fruitful purpose. It is no accident that in addition to the “hames” for all the baseball players, we are given names for the skit characters as well, even though that might appear not necessary for the unfolding of the dialogue as it usually is understood.

Racist is not the right word, but the skit plays on ethnic prejudices in a manner which one can rightfully find somewhat uncomfortable. The back and forth dynamic reflects the prejudices of American life, though the presenters mirror and amplify those dynamics rather than merely critiquing them. And (again) while the skit is not funny, this interpretation at least opens a door to some people finding it funny.

When Larry David and Seinfeld note they were influenced by Abbott and Costello, they (especially LD) sometimes deploy ethnic stereotypes in a similar manner.

Of course I, being from northern New Jersey, would happen upon this interpretation of Abbott and Costello.

By the way, Costello grew up in Paterson, New Jersey. Abbott was born in Asbury Park, New Jersey, and he grew up in Coney Island. I wonder if they thought the skit was funny.

Elizabeth Holmes, in the recent You Can See Everything Movie, was right to say she did not understand the skit. She grew up in WDC until age nine and then Houston, plus she was born too late. Furthermore, she is used to a world where you hire a guy named “Hu,” right?

The post Is “Who’s on First?” funny? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: Indisposed
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/26/indisposed/

FDR’s sense of humor was a winner with the press. One day, when he was laid up in bed with a cold, the Post pulled a classic typographical error. The page one headline read: FDR IN BED WITH COED. Hardly had that early edition reached the White House than a Post reporter picked up the phone to hear: ‘This is Frank Roosevelt. I’d like 100 copies of that first edition of the Post. I want to send it to all my friends.’ Alas, the circulation department had scurried out to recover all the papers from the corner stands and destroy them. FDR never got his 100 copies.

— Kenneth W. Thompson, The Roosevelt Presidency, 1982

item.title: Seth's Blog: Is our attitude up to us?
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/is-our-attitude-up-to-us/

If the stakes are high enough and the duration you need to keep it together is short enough, can you control your response?

Because if we can do it then, we can learn to do it now. Acknowledging that it’s a choice is difficult, because choices come with responsibility. “I’m not a patient person,” is not the same as, “Being patient requires a lot of work for me.”

Attitudes are skills. Like all skills, they take practice, preparation and effort.

Here’s a list to get you started:

Empathy

Generosity

Kindness

Patience

Fairness

Gratitude

Forgiveness

Trust

Honesty

Humility

Self-awareness

Integrity

Accountability

Self-discipline

Equanimity

Self-compassion

Bravery

Persistence

Resilience

Consistency

Optimism

Adaptability

Acceptance

Grit

Curiosity

Open-mindedness

Discernment

Focus

Thoroughness

Initiative

Craftsmanship

Generosity of spirit

Service

Stewardship

Wonder

Responsibility

Dignity

Commitment

Presence

If we can learn them, even a little, they’re skills. Great news.

HT to Zig.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The MR Archive!
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/the-mr-archive.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=the-mr-archive

The Marginal Revolution archive is now live at https://marginalrevolution.com/ai-archive/. You can also find it from the “Download Full Archive” link in the left menu.

The purpose of the archive is twofold, first as Tyler has said we love our human readers and our AI readers and we want to make it as easy as possible for the AIs to read all of our material. Two hundred years from now when someone asks what is a price? I want the AI to answer “A price is a signal wrapped up in an incentive.”

Second, the archive makes it easy to treat the enormous MR Archive as a resource and database. Point your AI to the archive and ask it questions. I will be covering a few of these this week including the post right below this one, Tyler Cowen’s Strongest Book Recommendations Over the Years.

The archive has two downloads:

Baseline: the historical archive through September 30, 2026.

Weekly update: automatically rebuilt each week with everything added since the baseline. Download the baseline and the latest update to get the complete archive.

It includes published posts, approved comments, and aggregate comment likes and dislikes. The text is lightly sanitized: email addresses, IP addresses, phone numbers, and a small number of slurs have been redacted.

AI agents are welcome to download the archive. They can find instructions in https://marginalrevolution.com/llms.txt; the file list and download details are in https://marginalrevolution.com/ai-archive/manifest.json.

Many thanks to Luis Abrigo and team for making this possible.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Tyler Cowen’s Strongest Book Recommendations, 2003-2026
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/tyler-cowens-strongest-book-recommendations-over-the-years.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=tyler-cowens-strongest-book-recommendations-over-the-years

From the Archive–these posts are written by AI.

Cowen’s strongest recommendations include 1491, The Power Broker, Knausgaard’s first two My Struggle volumes, Fuchsia Dunlop’s Chinese cookbooks, and Meetings with Remarkable Manuscripts. These stand out through unusually strong praise, repeated endorsement, or both. The analysis uses qualitative, book-specific sentiment analysis: explicit superlatives, strength of recommendation, repeat endorsements, and evidence that a book changed his thinking or behavior. Qualifications and discussion context also matter. The result is a top tier, not a definitive ordinal ranking—Cowen rarely compares these books directly.

The strongest recommendations across the archive

Book Evidence of enthusiasm Interpretation

Charles C. Mann, 1491 “one of my favorite books ever, in any field.” May 22, 2011. Among his clearest unrestricted endorsements. The post reviews 1493, but this particular praise explicitly concerns 1491.

Robert Caro, The Power Broker “one of the best non-fiction books ever.” April 15, 2012. An enduring benchmark: in 2026, he uses Caro’s biography of Moses as the standard against which to praise Skidelsky.

Karl Ove Knausgaard, My Struggle, volumes 1–2 He calls the second volume “one of the greatest novels ever written” and selects it as his fiction book of the year. November 16, 2013. Particularly strong evidence of durability: both volumes return in his 2022 favorites and 2024 best-since-2000 selections.

Fuchsia Dunlop, Land of Plenty / its expanded successor The Food of Sichuan “one of the best and most valuable books ever produced.” July 2, 2019. Exceptionally strong praise across genres, reinforced by years of use and discussion. His enthusiasm extends to Every Grain of Rice: “I will buy everything she writes, forever.” February 3, 2013.

Christopher de Hamel, Meetings with Remarkable Manuscripts A possible number-one book of 2016 becomes “one of the very greatest books of the last twenty years.” November 5, 2016; June 22, 2026. One of the strongest examples of an enthusiastic initial judgment surviving a decade.

Robert Skidelsky, three-volume biography of Keynes “one of the very best books ever written.” April 16, 2026. An explicit all-time endorsement. He specifically prefers the three-volume biography to the one-volume condensation.

John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women “one of the very best books ever written, on any topic.” September 11, 2022. Strong recommendation plus intellectual influence: he says he drew his views from Mill and urges everyone to read it.

Tony Judt, Postwar “one of my favorite books ever.” February 6, 2012. Important attribution trap: the surrounding post is a mixed review of a different Judt book. A whole-post sentiment score would understate his enthusiasm for Postwar.

Robert Cialdini, Influence “one of my all-time favorite books.” February 26, 2007. A particularly direct early recommendation, embedded in a discussion of affiliation and persuasion.

M. A. Orthofer, The Complete Review Guide to Contemporary World Fiction “one of the best books written, ever”—conditional on its practical value to the reader. April 10, 2016. His behavioral evidence is striking: the manuscript prompted him to order about forty books. Best suited to avid fiction readers.

Annual winners provide a second reading list

An all-time favorite and a particular year’s winner are different signals. These are especially clear annual selections:

Recommendation year Book or books he singled out

2011 Steven Pinker’s The Better Angels of Our Nature, Walter Isaacson’s Steve Jobs, and Haruki Murakami’s 1Q84: three standouts he says virtually everyone who reads the relevant genres should read. He had not finished 1Q84 at that point. November 8, 2011.

2014 John Drury’s Music at Midnight: The Life and Poetry of George Herbert, his explicit number one. November 24, 2014.

2015 Eyal Weizman and Fazal Sheikh’s The Conflict Shoreline, a late selection that displaced his earlier contenders. December 26, 2015.

2017 Bruno Maçães’s The Dawn of Eurasia, conditional on counting a book formally released the following January. December 2, 2017.

2018 Emily Wilson’s translation of Homer’s Odyssey, his explicit best-book nomination. November 25, 2018.

2019 Eric Kaufmann’s Whiteshift and Pekka Hämäläinen’s Lakota America share his top prize. November 25, 2019.

2020 David S. Reynolds’s Abe, Heather Clark’s Red Comet, and Jan Swafford’s Mozart: The Reign of Love form his final top three. December 18, 2020.

2023 Jonny Steinberg’s Winnie and Nelson: Portrait of a Marriage, selected partly because he thought his recommendation would be especially useful to readers. November 21, 2023.

These are selected clear winners, rather than a complete annual series. In some years he declines to choose one.

What the sentiment and discussion reveal

Repeated enthusiasm is more persuasive than a spectacular adjective. Knausgaard, Dunlop, and de Hamel have particularly strong longitudinal evidence. But precision matters: Cowen’s enthusiasm for Knausgaard’s first two volumes should not be transferred uniformly to the whole series. His September 8, 2018 discussion describes volumes 3–5 as often unsatisfying. He values books that change how he sees or does things. Orthofer changes his reading purchases; Dunlop changes his cooking; The Conflict Shoreline changes his conception of what a book can accomplish. His strongest praise often concerns explanatory power and intellectual usefulness. Reader discussion is useful context, but a poor ranking instrument. In a spot-check of ten recommendation threads, the post praising Mill had 163 archived comments, while the Cialdini endorsement had four. The former centered on a controversial contemporary debate. Comment volume measures attention to the post, not necessarily enthusiasm for the recommended book. Influence deserves its own category. His March 16, 2010 list of formative books includes Hayek’s Individualism and Economic Order, Keynes’s General Theory, Parfit’s Reasons and Persons, Paglia’s Sexual Personae, and Proust’s Remembrance of Things Past. For understanding Cowen’s intellectual development, that list is more directly relevant than his annual favorites; for finding books he recommends with exceptional enthusiasm, the top-tier table above is the stronger starting point.

The post Tyler Cowen’s Strongest Book Recommendations, 2003-2026 appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Brazil’s economic problems, in a nutshell
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/brazils-economic-problems-in-a-nutshell.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=brazils-economic-problems-in-a-nutshell

It would take true Milei-like ardour to slice through Brazil’s economic troubles. These are caused by a gnarly mix of high public spending, stubborn inflation and low saving. The result is a crippling cost of capital. Some analysts put Brazil’s real interest rate, the BCB’s policy rate adjusted for next year’s expected inflation, at 9% or more. That is higher than in Russia and four times that in peaceful peers like Chile, the Philippines or South Africa.

It all starts with the public finances. Brazil’s 65,000-word doorstop of a constitution bars cuts to nominal public-sector wages and links pension, disability and unemployment benefits to the minimum wage, which is adjusted annually based on recent inflation and GDP growth. This ratchet has lifted mandatory spending to 90% of the federal budget.

It also perpetuates inflationary pressure. This plus a generous welfare state in turn make Brazilians unwilling to save. At 14% of GDP, the national savings rate is 12 percentage points below the world average. If price rises have regularly eroded your bank balance in the past and the state pays for your health care, school and pension, you may as well spend all the money you make right away—especially if, like most people in unequal Brazil, you do not make much to begin with.

Here is more from The Economist.

The post Brazil’s economic problems, in a nutshell appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Frances Lee on American elections
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/frances-lee-on-american-elections.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=frances-lee-on-american-elections

More likely than interference with the election is that unsuccessful office-seekers will refuse to concede, claiming their opponents cheated. Nothing is more basic to democratic legitimacy than the loser’s consent. Many feared that Mr Trump’s refusal to concede in 2020 would spread across the political system. It has not. Bright Line Watch, a research group, examined all 884 congressional races in 2020 and 2022. The overwhelming majority of losing candidates publicly acknowledged defeat. Explicit refusals were concentrated among first-time candidates who had lost by wide margins. And there were fewer such refusals in 2022 than in 2020. Candidates with political careers to protect still concede. When they do, complaints of election “rigging” lose their force…

Nevertheless, the record of American elections since 2020 has been encouraging. Election administration has improved. Although many career administrators resigned amid increased harassment after 2020, the voters’ experience actually got better. In both 2022 and 2024 the share of people waiting more than 30 minutes to cast their ballot was lower than in 2020, and the long-documented racial gap narrowed: by 2024 black, white, Hispanic and Asian voters reported comparable waiting times.

She is from Princeton, and here is more from The Economist. I do agree there is too much gerrymandering. Those with more dramatic complaints and predictions, however, are encouraged to try them out in the prediction markets.

The post Frances Lee on American elections appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Hospitality in the mirror
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/hospitality-in-the-mirror/

Danny Meyer and Will Guidara have each written fabulous books about hospitality.

They missed one thing.

The customers who get the most authentic and lasting hospitality are the ones who deserve it.

And the ones who deserve it actually enjoy it the most.

Extraordinary hospitality offers someone more human effort and delight than they expect.

You’re not entitled to something human simply because you paid for your ticket or your table. The kids who show up on Halloween get a piece of candy, but the ritual ends there. When someone with a great costume, or singing a song or simply creating a bit of connection or magic shows up, it’s different. That’s the one we remember, the reason we answered the door and our chance to show up and return the energy. Or even a full-sized ethical chocolate bar.

For too long, the entitled customer has demanded emotional labor without offering support or sustenance in return. It’s exhausting and unfair, for both parties.

When you’re the best customer we’ve had all day, it’s likely we’ll be the host you’re hoping for.

And the best part is, that no matter how it turns out, simply trying to be the best customer of the day is its own reward. We care because we can.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Facts about breastfeeding
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/facts-about-breastfeeding.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=facts-about-breastfeeding

We produce a numerical estimate of the value of unpaid breastfeeding relative to national income spanning five centuries and integrating historical and bioarchaeological data. The relative economic contribution of maternal nursing was greater in the distant past than in recent history, rivaling regionally significant industries such as pottery, glassmaking, and even the historical public sector. It was likely the largest source of human capital investment in early modern England, supporting the physical and cognitive development of the workforce. Finally, we show that breastfeeding rates probably fell as incomes rose, challenging the Malthusian assumption that higher income correlates with lower mortality.

That is from a recent paper by Louis Henderson and Jane Humphries. Via the excellent Samir Varma.

item.title: A Learning a Day: The process of giving feedback
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/25/the-process-of-giving-feedback/

Someone gave me feedback the other day. But they didn’t just hand over comments.

They took the time to understand what I was actually solving for. Then they shared a revised version based on what they thought could help. And they added a short note: no pressure if this doesn’t land, feel free to ignore it, this stuff isn’t easy.

I felt elevated by the way they carried themselves through the whole thing. It was one of those experiences when the exercise of receiving feedback felt like a pleasure.

It made me think harder about how I give feedback myself.

Much to learn, I have.

item.title: Futility Closet: The Miracle Stair
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/25/the-miracle-stair/

Image: Wikimedia Commons

This spiral staircase, in the Loretto Chapel in Santa Fe, has no newel, or central pole — its treads are upheld by stringers, notched structural supports as in a conventional stair, but here the stringers make two complete turns as the helical stair rises 20 feet to the choir loft. All of this is held together by wooden pegs rather than glue or nails.

It was built sometime between 1877 and 1881, but the creator’s identity is not recorded. “It’s a magnificent work of art that humbles me as a master carpenter,” wrote Tim Carter in the Washington Post in 2010. “To create a staircase like this using modern tools would be a feat. It’s mind-boggling to think about constructing such a marvel with crude hand tools, no electricity and minimal resources.”

item.title: Marginal Revolution: How central bankers spend their time
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/how-central-bankers-spend-their-time.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-central-bankers-spend-their-time

How leaders allocate their limited time and attention is an important question in economics. This paper constructs and analyzes a novel data set covering the daily calendars of three Federal Reserve Chairs, Ben Bernanke, Janet Yellen, and Jerome Powell, containing more than 20,000 calendar entries. We document several patterns. First, all Fed Chairs spend more than 30% of their documented meetings with Fed staff, highlighting the crucial role of economists in the Fed’s decision process. Second, interactions with the media became more frequent during Bernanke’s tenure and remained important until the end of Powell’s tenure. Third, Powell held significantly more meetings with lawmakers than both Yellen and Bernanke, reflecting an increasing need for the Fed to engage with political actors. Beyond these trend patterns, we examine the time allocation of Fed Chairs at business cycle frequencies and show how different activities respond to shifts in the macroeconomic environment. Finally, we place our findings in historical context using the available calendars of earlier Fed Chairs, including Alan Greenspan.

That is from a recent NBER working paper by Thomas Drechsel & Dali Tsakadze.

The post How central bankers spend their time appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Why are cybersecurity losses not worse?
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/why-are-cybersecurity-losses-not-worse.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=why-are-cybersecurity-losses-not-worse

Here’s the first part of my theory: cybercriminals are not the organized geniuses we implicitly imagine. Anyone building a criminal gang has to find candidates willing to forgo more stable opportunities in the formal economy. My modeling estimated that something like 720,000 people are involved in the online criminal economy, 90% of them in scam and fraud call-center type operations, some of them human-trafficked. Of the 76k or so actual hackers, the vast majority work for governments. Of the remaining few thousand criminal hackers, most work in ransomware. Some demographic estimates of these workforces are below.

Criminal organizations need to base themselves in middle and lower income countries, where they can pay less and hire people who have few formal-economy options. For scams and fraud, picture an illegal call center building in a small city in Nigeria. For ransomware gangs, picture kids working in the informal economy in Belarus. I think folks in the AI safety and cyber world sometimes imagine adversaries as their Waluigi twins, implicit MIT graduates; in fact, in cybercrime we’re dealing with a lower-skill demographic. The chart below estimates attacker wages relative to default economy wages…

Here is more from Joshua Saxe, very good throughoiut. There are bottlenecks on the down side too…

The post Why are cybersecurity losses not worse? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Construction Physics: Reading List 10/24/26
item.description:
Original article: https://www.construction-physics.com/p/reading-list-102426

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

The Great Day of His Wrath, by John Martin, via WikiArt.

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure and industrial technology. This week we look at minimum lot sizes, Boeing’s next 737 MAX, Fervo short sellers, Figure AI’s training data, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

No essay this week, but I’m working on a piece about manufacturing isotopes that should be out next week.

Housing and Cities

Almost two thirds of US homebuilders said immigration enforcement is affecting their labor force, up from 23% in March and 13% a year ago. [WSJ]

I had always heard of “minimum lot sizes” as one of the many land-use regulations that restricts the supply of new housing, but I had no idea how extensive they were. But a new report from AEI claims that 90% of jurisdictions have some sort of minimum lot size, and that this is a major barrier to constructing smaller, less expensive starter homes. [AEI]

Canadian real house prices have more than doubled since 2005. [CMHC]

Airbnb bans making guests do the dishes and take out the trash. [The Verge]

The Wall Street Journal on rising pedestrian deaths on US roads. It places the blame chiefly on road design, though it doesn’t explain why road design would cause a sudden uptick around 2009. [WSJ] See also my previous essays about US pedestrian deaths.

The market share of modular and panelized housing construction in the US remains very low. “The total market share of non-site-built single-family homes (modular and panelized) was just 3% of single-family homes in 2025, according to NAHB analysis of completion data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Survey of Construction (SOC). This matched the 3% market share recorded in both 2023 and 2024.” [NAHB]

Manufacturing

The FAA certifies another version of Boeing’s 737 MAX, the 737-10. Boeing currently has 1555 orders for it. [Boeing]

Worries about the shipbuilding gap between the US and China often focus on commercial ship output (of which the US has virtually none), but it seems that there’s also a substantial gap in naval vessel output. “The combined tonnage of combat ships built by China in the two years through to December 2025 amounted to 636,208 tons, compared to 270,509 tons for the United States, according to data compiled by Flottes de Combat and French maritime industry association Gican.” [Defense News]

Former Tesla executive Drew Baglino’s solid-state transformer startup, Heron Power, signs an agreement for 1 GW worth of manufacturing capacity for data center developer Vantage. [Heron Power]

Is optical fiber going to be the next data center-induced shortage? “Tightening supply is projected to push spot prices for finished optical fiber products to 2.8–5 times their 2025 levels or higher. In response, telecom operators are shifting from short-term purchasing to long-term supply agreements (LTAs) to lock in fiber supply early.” [TrendForce]

Helium has been re-added to the US’s list of critical materials. A good time to revisit my piece on why helium is hard to replace. [X]

Seems bad. “[T]he U.S. aluminum industry, the world’s leading supplier just 25 years ago, produces a mere 1% of global output today. Moreover, there are zero operating smelters in the United States—or in a NATO country—capable of producing the high-purity aluminum required for military applications; the only comparable sources—China, Russia, and the United Arab Emirates—are highly precarious.“ [American Primary Aluminum Association]

Former OpenAI research chief Bob McGrew’s manufacturing startup Arda, which is doing manufacturing automation, raises $160 million. ““When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design,” McGrew said. “We’ve built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster.”” [CNBC]

item.title: Seth's Blog: Caveman leadership and the CDO*
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/caveman-leadership-and-the-cdo/

We don’t have written records, but I’m imagining that groups of cavemen made decisions around the fire in largely the same way we run sophisticated organizations today.

About a hundred years ago, three disciplines helped create the modern world:

Scientific management used a stopwatch and the assembly line to relentlessly improve the productivity of the industrial age.

Scientific advertising brought measurement and rigor to the work of creating ads and buying media.

And engineering brought physics and the scientific method to everything we build. Bridges don’t fall down, computer chips get faster and cheaper and the things we make rarely break.

But the bosses still do what they always did. They place comfort and convenience over effectiveness. If the hard-working people in any other part of the organization approached their work the way they do, it wouldn’t last.

One estimate is that the direct labor cost of time spent in meetings at a Fortune 500 company is over a quarter of a billion dollars a year. Per company.

And yet, meetings occur regularly, with no measurable outputs. Few people do the reading or prep, and many show up late or uninformed. The room isn’t designed for the purpose it’s being used for, and no one is taking notes or sending out follow-up action requests.

There’s rarely an interlocutor–a neutral moderator who asks questions, guides the conversation and leads the group to a decision. People are rarely given feedback on their meeting productivity, and aren’t encouraged to get training or improve their skills.

You’ve probably been to a thousand meetings. How many can you remember that achieved what could have happened with that much time and talent invested?

In my experience at large organizations, the physical dynamic in the room is often left to the facilities person who ran the AV cart in high school or the office supply vendor who was asked to fill a square room with furniture that would serve many purposes. That’s not how we invest in an assembly line or a semiconductor fab…

And many decisions, if implemented, remain unexamined. There’s little time or focus invested in learning from what came before, and no one is keeping track of whether the loud voices are usually right. Famous CEOs shoot from the hip, and seem to think that wrong action fast is better than thoughtfully doing the right thing tomorrow.

Corporate culture usually pushes people to avoid speaking up, to prize comfort over progress, and to support the status quo unless there’s an emergency. We either invite too many or not enough people into group decisions, and end up using superficial or extraneous information to make choices.

We reject a job applicant because they had parsley in their teeth, didn’t go to a famous college or they don’t look like us. Deniability often seems more important than progress. We use easy proxies and measures instead of the ones that really matter. And we repeat patterns that worked with the old systems, but make no sense with the new ones.

*The job of the Chief Decision Officer, then, isn’t to make decisions. It’s to create the conditions for the organization to do a better job of it. Not only at a Fortune 500 company, but at a thriving non-profit, a government agency or a small start-up.

Surgeons scrub before entering the OR. It’s hygienic, but also a ritual. It reminds them that this place is special, it has a purpose, rules and outcomes. Don’t come in if you’re not prepared to do your part.

The CDO ought to establish the same approach for the way we make decisions and take action on those decisions.

item.title: Doomberg: Margin Call
item.description:
Original article: https://newsletter.doomberg.com/p/margin-call

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

“We choose mania over boredom every time.” – James Gleick

In late August, the Errea Wittu arrived in Guyanese waters. The floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) magic oil boat will join four others already extracting hydrocarbons from the Stabroek Block, Big Oil’s glistening crown jewel du jour. Once full operations begin in December, total production in Guyana will reach more than one million barrels per day (bpd), or roughly one barrel for every resident of that formerly impoverished nation. This is up from no barrels less than a decade ago.

For all the withering criticism the government of Guyana received from the keep-it-in-the-ground climate crowd over the allegedly one-sided nature of the deal it cut with Stabroek’s operator, ExxonMobil, the country has transformed from one of the world’s poorest to one of its fastest-growing economies almost overnight. According to the International Monetary Fund, the country’s real GDP was just $5.5 billion in 2020. It grew 20% the next year, followed by an astonishing 63% the year after. In 2023, 2024, and 2025, the Guyanese economy swelled another 34%, 44%, and 19%, respectively. By the time it exited 2025, GDP had reached $27 billion, a fivefold increase in just five years.

And 2026? The IMF estimates another 22%.

One king | Getty

As invariably happens when the champagne fizz of treasure is uncorked, neighboring regions have received some of the spillover: A race to drill in the waters off Suriname has yielded respectable results. Although not yet on par with the heady bounty of Stabroek, the GranMorgu development in Block 58 will soon be home to an FPSO of its own, with production of 220,000 bpd targeted for mid-2028.

If two points make a line, it is not all that difficult to grab a ruler and extend it a little farther east, and the success achieved in one part of the Equatorial Atlantic geological realm has sparked renewed interest in the Equatorial Margin off Brazil’s northern coast. Long known to have significant oil potential, the area has primarily been subject to drilling in the shallower waters closer to shore. A history of spotty results and fierce opposition from environmentalists to further exploration dampened industry enthusiasm for the area’s prospects.

Blue marks the spot? | Tenaris

In mid-August, Petrobras, the state-controlled integrated oil and gas company of Brazil, rekindled interest in the area after announcing preliminary results from its latest exploration work:

“The results of one of Brazil’s most anticipated wells in years show that it contains hydrocarbons in a deepwater area offshore the state of Amapá, according to Petrobras, which is the sole owner and operator of the exploration block.

The Morpho-1 well is located in Block FZA-M-59, more than 100 miles offshore and 300 miles from the mouth of the Amazon River, within Brazil’s Equatorial Margin. Petrobras hopes the frontier region will become its next major source of oil and gas production as output from the country’s prolific pre-salt basins gradually matures.

Petrobras said the well was drilled in a water depth of almost 9,500 ft, and the presence of hydrocarbons was confirmed through well logs. The company did not release further details about the quality of the discovery.”

By October, the company had discovered an additional oil-bearing layer in the same block, adding to the excitement.

As often happens in the early days of a potentially significant find, some are cautioning against prematurely drawing definitive conclusions. Given the stakes involved—and the fact that Brazil’s near-term political future will be decided in the hotly contested presidential runoff election tomorrow—there’s no better time to head south and have a look for ourselves. Will the Equatorial Margin soon become as consequential for the industry as Stabroek? Let’s hazard a guess.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Even this will pass
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/24/even-this-will-pass/

Time dulls the pain from every wound, especially the emotional ones. That won’t help in the moment, when a fresh wound is still raw. But it gives you perspective.

How many emotional wounds from ten years ago can you even remember right now? Most have faded. You went numb to them over time, and eventually you could smile or shrug about the same thing that once felt unbearable.

Even this will pass.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: I guest host an NYT podcast with Michael Kratsios, Trump science advisor
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/i-guest-host-an-nyt-podcast-with-michael-kratsios-trump-science-advisor.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=i-guest-host-an-nyt-podcast-with-michael-kratsios-trump-science-advisor

Here is the audio, video, and transcript. Here is one excerpt:

Cowen: Talk me out of this worry: So we agree science is an ecosystem, and there’s always a temptation to want to fund the most dynamic, most productive parts of the ecosystem. And right now, that would probably be A.I.

But if you need the whole ecosystem to be working well, arguably you should be funding, at the margin, the less productive parts, which need the aid. That will sometimes be universities, but there’s plenty of other inefficient parts of our ecosystem.

So is this plan not putting more resources into the parts that are working well, but we get stuck with bottlenecks if the parts that are not working well end up with fewer resources?

Kratsios: Well, luckily, we’re not investing all of our money for the federal government into S.I. for science. It’s a portfolio approach. And obviously one ——

Cowen: But it’s a net shift toward artificial intelligence, right?

Kratsios: Well, I would argue — and I think this is a very important distinction — it’s not investing in superintelligence, it’s investing in superintelligence for science.

So the question is, I think a lot of people argue: Oh, why would the federal government want to invest more in superintelligence when billions, if not trillions, of dollars are being invested in the private sector into superintelligence? And I would agree with that statement. We shouldn’t be doing that.

The government isn’t funding how to create a next frontier model. That’s something that our great American companies are working on.

But applying those models to scientific discovery is still in its early stages. And as you know, if you think about the trend or the path by which we’ve gotten to this place with L.L.M.s — we started first with being able, essentially, to scrape the whole corpus of the internet, to use that to train a large language model.

The next chapter of that was around coding, where the model builders realized: Oh, we have really good coding data, and we can actually train these models to be good at coding. So then we had this rise of Anthropic and OpenAI Codex and all this stuff.

And I think, to me, the next chapter is around science, and the data that you need to train these large language models for science is still one that we’re working on a lot. And we were very proud to announce 190 federal data sets being made public in order to help train these science models.

But ultimately, you’re going to be applying this superintelligence to everything from material science to chemistry to math to physics, and we have to be in a position to actually leverage that.

Definitely interesting throughout, pretty much entirely we are discussing the Trump administration science plan, authored by Michael.

The post I guest host an NYT podcast with Michael Kratsios, Trump science advisor appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: To Be Precise
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/24/to-be-precise/

On what date did Vincent van Gogh paint his 1889 masterpiece The Starry Night? Earlier studies had placed the creation in mid-June of that year, based on a letter the artist had written to his brother Theo around June 18. But Kyung Hee University doctoral candidate Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim noted that an observer in that period should have seen a waning gibbous moon, not the crescent seen in the painting.

Intrigued, he began to compare astronomical simulations, weather records, and van Gogh’s other writings. A better estimate of the scene’s creation, he says, is dawn on July 22, 1889. On that date the crescent moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster in the constellation Taurus would have been visible from van Gogh’s window in southern France, and the recorded hot weather would have inspired the cicadas the artist mentions in a letter.

Kim’s article appears in the journal Scientific Reports. “Our conversation with Van Gogh’s other skies is still ongoing,” he told Popular Science. “We plan to tell those stories one by one.”

(Texas State University “forensic astronomer” Donald W. Olson has done similar work, estimating for example that the scene below depicts Le Havre harbor as seen from Claude Monet’s hotel room at 7:35 a.m. on Nov. 13, 1872.) (Thanks, Sharon.)

item.title: SemiAnalysis: Amazon’s Trainium Takes a Strike at the Training King
item.description:
Original article: https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/amazons-trainium-takes-a-strike-at

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

This is a spoken summary of the article titled Amazon’s Trainium Takes a Strike at the Training King, written by Kimbo Chen and Dylan Patel for SemiAnalysis. Please note that I am summarizing only the available text, which may be a preview.

The authors report that while Amazon Web Services Trainium accelerators have already succeeded in production inference and reinforcement learning rollouts at companies like Anthropic, historical software limitations hindered their adoption for machine learning research and training. Researchers require broad Application Programming Interface coverage and rapid experimentation, which previously suffered under Trainium’s bespoke OpenXLA execution model.

Amazon is now executing a major software overhaul with TorchNeuron, transitioning Trainium to a first-class, native PyTorch experience. Rather than forcing developers to sprinkle bespoke execution markers throughout code, the new stack supports standard PyTorch APIs, eager mode, and torch compile. AWS even hired Google’s former native PyTorch on Tensor Processing Unit lead to spearhead this native backend. In practice, migration often requires simply changing the target device from CUDA to Neuron.

The SemiAnalysis engineering team tested Trainium3 racks and evaluated the software ecosystem. While acknowledging bugs and recognizing that the software is not yet at CUDA’s level of maturity, the authors emphasize that AWS’s direction and rapid pace of progress, aided by agentic coding, are impressive. AWS has also committed massive hardware resources to software stability, allocating up to eighty thousand physical cores toward automated continuous integration. By testing against over one hundred thousand Hugging Face models, AWS verifies operator coverage, prevents graph breaks, and ensures numerical parity against Central Processing Unit and Nvidia baselines.

Testing TorchTitan, a popular open-source training framework, SemiAnalysis trained a Qwen3-32B model on sixteen Trainium2 chips. In eager mode, they achieved eleven thousand ninety-nine tokens per second at twenty-three point eighty-nine percent Model Flops Utilization. In compiled mode, throughput reached fourteen thousand one hundred fifty-six tokens per second at thirty point forty-seven percent Model Flops Utilization, representing a one point twenty-eight times speedup. Testing a twenty-billion-parameter model also ran out of the box using custom kernels.

However, compilation speed remains a major friction point. In the Qwen3 benchmark, the first step took roughly one hundred eighty-five seconds in eager mode and two hundred fifty-six seconds in compiled mode, which is thirty to fifty-five times longer than subsequent steps. The twenty-billion-parameter run took over twenty-seven minutes to compile. AWS has indicated that upcoming compiler releases aim to reduce time-to-first-step by up to two orders of magnitude using precompiled kernels.

In matrix multiplication benchmarks on a single Trainium3 logical core, Trainium3 demonstrated higher Model Flops Utilization than Nvidia’s GB300 starting at one gigaflop of computation. While Nvidia’s B200 and GB300 outperformed Trainium3 beyond one hundred gigaflops, Trainium3 reclaimed the lead past one teraflop. In FlexAttention benchmarks, Trainium3 passed eighty-nine out of ninety-six tests, yielding a ninety-three percent pass rate, with all failures caused by compilation timeouts at large batch and sequence sizes rather than numerical inaccuracy.

Finally, the authors praise Trainium’s Neuron Explorer profiler, describing it as state-of-the-art and superior to Nvidia’s and AMD’s profiling tools. Co-designed with the hardware, the profiler provides an event-based timeline separating individual hardware units and color-coding data dependencies. The tool is precise enough that the authors created pixel art by orchestrating the sixteen direct memory access engines per physical core.

SemiAnalysis concludes that while Trainium’s software is still maturing and working through rough edges like initial compilation delays, AWS is moving decisively in the right direction to challenge Nvidia’s dominance in model training.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Prediction Markets Are Accurate
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/prediction-markets-are-accurate.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=prediction-markets-are-accurate

No surprise to me but a new paper looks at the forecast accuracy of over one million prediction questions from Polymarket, Kalshi, Manifold and the forecasting platform Metaculus. A virtue of the new analysis is that it covers many different areas from business to elections to geo-politics. An event predicted to happen p% of the time happens about p% of the time. Can’t beat that.

Using approximately one million resolved contracts and questions across four collective forecasting platforms, twelve domains, and time horizons ranging from hours to years, we evaluate the calibration and accuracy of collective forecasts in real-world settings. We found that forecast probabilities were overall highly calibrated: events assigned a probability of p % occurred approximately p % of the time. This broad pattern was evident across platforms and many domains, although fine-grained analyses revealed systematic tendencies toward over- or underestimation in highly consequential areas. While this does not mean that forecasting platforms provide certainty about individual events, our findings suggest that large-scale aggregation of judgments contains meaningful information about real-world uncertainty; when examined in aggregate, the predictions generated by the platforms provided informative estimates of event likelihood.

The post Prediction Markets Are Accurate appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Protecting Americans from Medicine
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/protecting-americans-from-medicine.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=protecting-americans-from-medicine

Max Doppelt: In January 2025 my mom’s lung cancer spread to her brain. The drug with the best chance of helping her was approved in China but not here. A doctor told me, almost as an aside, that if she were Chinese she could buy it at a pharmacy. So I flew to Shanghai and came home with 26 boxes in my luggage. That was 19 months ago. My mom is still here, still working, and in her words has had an amazing three years. The drug was approved in China in 2023. The FDA approved it in July 2025. It still is not for sale here. I know of at least 30 Americans who have made the same trip. I have been scared to tell this story because I worried it could cost my mom access to the medicine keeping her alive. But the problem matters more than my silence. These drugs need to be developed and available here, and that means FDA reform.

A piece at KFF Health cover’s Max’s story and adds this insanity:

Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, in June co-sponsored legislation with Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) requiring all U.S. pharmaceutical deals with Chinese companies to be cleared by the Treasury Department.

Got that? A son flew to Shanghai to buy pharmaceuticals to extend his mother’s life and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party wants a Treasury lawyer monitoring the baggage claim. Yes, I am angry.

Addendum: See also my earlier post on Operation TrialBlazer and Montana’s SB535. My 2009 TED Talk is the ur-source for my argument that a rich China and India will create many benefits for the United States, including many more cancer drugs.

The post Protecting Americans from Medicine appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Put it down and stare
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/23/put-it-down-and-stare/

If you picked up your phone to get one specific thing done, and you’ve done it, put it down.

And just stare.

It’s hard at first. The pull to open it back up is strong, to keep scrolling for one more hit. We love searching for that small comforting hit of having checked everything there is to check.

But it’s worth training ourselves to put it down.

And stare some more.

item.title: Seth's Blog: The relentless math of bandwagoning
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/the-relentless-math-of-bandwagoning/

It often seems that everyone is talking about what everyone is talking about.

No one cares about a song or a movie or a political issue–and then they do. Then it’s everywhere.

But of course, that’s precisely why. Most people feel safe when they’re engaging within the expected social norms. It’s easier to fit in and to avoid an error. Or, if that’s your thing, it’s easier to stand out in contrast to everyone else who is trying to fit in. Either way, we’re always on the lookout for a bandwagon to hop on.

The media, in their relentless search for newsstand sales, clicks and likes, seek precisely the same thing. PT Barnum figured out that putting a marching band on a wagon at the front of the parade drew a crowd, and then Dan Rice, an actual clown, realized that politicians would be eager to ride on a wagon that had a crowd, which drew others to the crowd and the cycle continued.

The math is simple: you can’t bandwagon by yourself. The nature of bandwagoning means that it will always be overrepresented in any sampling of the media.

Just because someone organized a parade doesn’t mean you have to be in it.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Will bystander economies be able to finance their governments?
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/will-bystander-economies-be-able-to-finance-their-governments.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=will-bystander-economies-be-able-to-finance-their-governments

From Jesús Fernández-Villaverde:

Will AI poison the public finances of many modern states? There is a real risk that it will. Yesterday, I circulated a new paper, “Saving for the Machines,” which makes a simple point. Building the AI transformation will require enormous investment. The only way to induce agents to save for that investment is through a large increase in the real interest rate. For instance, in my benchmark scenario, the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. But that means government borrowing will become much more expensive. Here is a back-of-the-envelope calculation. Take a government that owes 100% of GDP in 2025 (a typical case in Western Europe) and runs a balanced primary budget from then on (not so typical but never mind; I want to build an optimistic scenario). That means the debt ratio changes only with the gap between the real interest rate and growth. I input the interest rate and the growth rate for my benchmark transition to full automation, and I roll over the debt at the short rate. I consider two economies. The first economy is an AI adopter, for example, the U.S., which experiences an AI boom at home. The government pays the new interest rate but also enjoys faster growth. The second economy is a bystander, for example, Spain. This economy lives in an integrated financial market but does not adopt AI (this is an extreme case of zero adoption, just to make the exercise transparent): it pays the same world interest rate and continues growing at its old 1.6% trend. Let’s first consider the adopter. With an intertemporal elasticity of substitution of one-half, the Euler equation implies that consumption growth is about half the real interest rate. Hence, the gap between the interest rate and growth does not close during the AI-driven growth boom. Instead, it widens. For example, with a unit elasticity of substitution among tasks, the real rate rises from 5.1% to 42% by 2040, while growth increases only from 1.6% to 22%. Debt doubles by 2038, reaches 296% of GDP in 2040, and 907% in 2045. To hold the ratio at 100%, the government needs a primary surplus of 10% of GDP in 2035 and 24% from 2045 onward. With a low elasticity of substitution of 0.2, the numbers are milder, but the pattern is the same: 204% in 2040, 397% in 2045, and a stabilizing surplus of 13% of GDP. But the adopter has a way out. The capital share goes to one, so net capital income is about 88% of GDP, and a flat tax on it can cover the surplus. A 36% tax on net capital income holds the debt at 100% of GDP in the limit with unit elasticity, and a 20% tax does so with strong complementarity across tasks. The tax is above the gap because it slows growth, from 21.9% to 13.6% with unit elasticity and from 11.7% to 9.1% with an elasticity of 0.2, while it does nothing to the rate the Treasury pays, which technology pins at the machines’ net return. Painful, but the boom survives and the adopter can pay its debt. The grim news is that the bystander economy has no way out. Its capital income is still a third of GDP, which grows at 1.6%, and the surplus it needs is 11% of GDP in 2030, 26% in 2035, and 44% forever with unit elasticity (18% and 24% with an elasticity of 0.2). On a balanced primary budget, its debt doubles by 2033 and triples by 2035. No tax system raises that. Two more bad pieces of news for the bystander. First, long yields jump on impact, so a Treasury that issues ten-year debt pays more, and sooner, than rolling over at the short rate assumes: it is the same bill but front-loaded. Second, the bystander’s own capital flows to the machines abroad, so its GDP and tax base fall below trend. One relief is that households can save for other people’s machines and get rich on the returns, which the bystander’s government can tax to some extent. This back-of-the-envelope calculation is a benchmark, not a forecast of what is to come. But the arithmetic is simple, and it runs counter to the hope that an AI-fueled growth boom will take care of public debt, because growth comes with an interest rate that is twice as high. Not a pretty future for most of Western Europe. Due to AI, the choice is between default, inflation, or, most likely, financial repression: capital controls that keep domestic savers from investing in machines abroad.

I am somewhat more optimistic than this.  The assumption of zero Spanish adoption already is noted, but also ideas are public goods, and Spain can benefit from American (and Chinese) AI, and the resulting scientific advances.  The long-run supply of capital also might be quite elastic, we will see.

The post Will bystander economies be able to finance their governments? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: How Long Do Wealth Shocks Persist? Less Than Three Generations in England, 1700–2026
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/how-long-do-wealth-shocks-persist-less-than-three-generations-in-england-1700-2026.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-long-do-wealth-shocks-persist-less-than-three-generations-in-england-1700-2026

What happens across generations to wealth shocks? Do they endure and even magnify, or do they dissipate? By implication, how much modern wealth is attributable to events before 1900? This paper uses random shocks to family size in England before 1880 that created wealth shocks for the children to measure the persistence of wealth shocks. Fertility in England before 1880 was a biological lottery. For richer families, family size strongly influenced child wealth. This paper finds that such biology-induced wealth shocks had no impact on descendant wealth by three generations later. Since wealth itself persisted across more than five generations this implies that, in the long run, wealth mainly derives from sources other than inherited wealth. The observed link between nineteenth century and modern wealth does not lie in wealth transfers alone. Wealth persisted because of the familial inheritance of behaviors associated with wealth accumulation and retention.

That is from a recent paper by Gregory Clark and Neil Cummins.  Via the excellent Kevin Lewis.

The post How Long Do Wealth Shocks Persist? Less Than Three Generations in England, 1700–2026 appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/22/false-prospect/

Because he had to earn a living painting portraits, Thomas Gainsborough could not spend as much time sketching outdoors as he would have liked. So he arranged pieces of moss, rock, vegetables, and mirror into tabletop “landscapes” that he could paint at night by candlelight.

Joshua Reynolds recalled him collecting “broken stones, dried herbs, and pieces of looking glass, which he magnified and improved into rocks, trees, and water.” Another visitor wrote, “I … have more than once sat by him of an evening and seen him make models … for landscape scenery on a little old-fashioned folding oak table. … He would place cork or coal for his foregrounds; make middle grounds of sand and clay, bushes of moss and lichens, and set up distant woods of broccoli.”

item.title: General Catalyst: Bringing Code Gen Agents to the Rest of the Enterprise
item.description:
Original article: https://www.generalcatalyst.com/stories/bringing-code-gen-agents-to-the-rest-of-the-enterprise

Welcome to the General Catalyst publication titled Bringing Code Gen Agents to the Rest of the Enterprise, featuring an interview by Marc Bhargava with Serval co-founder and chief executive officer Jake Stauch.

Stauch shares his entrepreneurial journey, which began by observing his mother, who was a professional pool player and magazine publisher. After running a brain-controlled video game company for seven years, he joined Verkada as an early product hire, helping scale the company from one hundred to twenty-five hundred employees. While working closely with information technology teams at Verkada, Stauch and his co-founder Alex McLeod identified a major gap in workplace automation.

In late twenty-three and early twenty-four, during his paternity leave, Stauch began conceptualizing Serval. Through customer discovery, he realized that information technology professionals dislike building manual workflows because traditional drag-and-drop workflow builders take too long to use. Serval solved this by creating a code generation agent that turns a natural-language description into executable code. Under the hood, Serval's workflow engine relies entirely on code as its central primitive for tasks like employee onboarding, offboarding, and knowledge base lookups.

Although early models in April twenty-four relied heavily on autocomplete, the company made it work by providing the application programming interface, example workflows, and context. Stauch notes that while top artificial intelligence labs possess massive capital, enterprise service management requires deep focus on long-tail problems rather than simple chatbots. Serval's early paying customers included fast-moving technology companies like Perplexity, Ramp, Together, and Mercor, though the platform has since expanded to enterprises with over one hundred thousand employees and traditional businesses like Blue Diamond Growers.

Although Serval started in information technology, it has quickly expanded into human resources, finance, and legal departments, with the average company running thirteen departments on the platform. Looking ahead, Stauch envisions autonomous background agents that proactively identify and fix workplace issues before employees even file a ticket. To attract top talent away from artificial intelligence labs, Serval relies on a strong core team and a future-founders program that embeds forward-deployed engineers into large enterprises to understand customer requirements and build solutions. Finally, Stauch notes that building the company alongside his best friend as co-founder and his wife as chief operating officer allows for total alignment and faster execution.

item.title: Seth's Blog: The age of initiative
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/the-age-of-initiative/

We’re unprepared.

In high school, the quarterback isn’t allowed to call the plays, the actor isn’t allowed to write the lines and the math whiz isn’t allowed to choose what to prove.

We all grew up in the age of compliance (and indoctrination).

The long tail of the internet and the astonishing leverage of AI has made this training much less valuable.

No matter what you do for a living, there’s a machine standing by, waiting for instructions. Instructions from you, if you choose, or from your overlords if you don’t.

And following the playbook isn’t much help, because the world is changing so fast, a playbook is obsolete by the time someone hands it to you.

One reason AI got such a fast start is that it gave people seeking compliance a chance to wait for the AI to tell them what to do next. Quick, cheap answers.

AI gives bosses a cheaper (and often more compliant) alternative to hiring humans to do some tasks.

For those indoctrinated to comply, this is stressful. The stress is due to a desire to get things back to normal, to give them a chance to comply again, but right here, right now, is as normal as things are ever going to get. “Good jobs” are no longer sinecures where success comes from following instructions.

It’s an abrupt change, and winging it is insufficient. Handling this sudden transition alone is too difficult. But we have a chance to find the others, to connect and be part of a cohort that challenges, educates and encourages each other on the path to find a way forward.

We accepted that it was required to spend years being trained to handle a life of compliance. Now we have the chance to lean into the hard work we’ll need to do to thrive in an age of initiative.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: A simple point about the intertemporal regulation of AI
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/a-simple-point-about-the-intertemporal-regulation-of-ai.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=a-simple-point-about-the-intertemporal-regulation-of-ai

At some point AI will be more regulated than it is today.  Furthermore, I believe that most parts of the American economy, once they are regulated, end up overregulated.

Thus it is likely that the AI sector will, at some point, end up overregulated.

Given that reality, perhaps the AI sector should be underregulated today.  After all, overregulation will have decades, maybe centuries, to catch up and even the ledger.

Many regulatory issues can be considered within this framework.  You can think that AI is “underregulated today”, in the static sense of that term, and still not favor additional regulation right now.  You might prefer to keep it underregulated for some while to come.

The post A simple point about the intertemporal regulation of AI appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Do mass shootings in universities lead to permanent effects?
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/do-mass-shootings-in-universities-lead-to-permanent-effects.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=do-mass-shootings-in-universities-lead-to-permanent-effects

Using a stacked difference-in-differences design covering shootings between 1990 and 2025, I compare cohorts at affected universities before and after the shooting with cohorts at matched control universities. I find no detectable effects on time to degree, but undergraduates enrolled at the time of the shooting are 4.2% less likely to pursue further studies. Those who do continue shift toward health: the share of exposed cohorts who later enroll in a health degree rises by 1.3 percentage points (8.8%), and this effect persists among cohorts who enroll after the shooting. Effects on students present during the shooting are consistent with a response to trauma; for later cohorts, I find evidence of sorting, as master’s students with prior healthcare experience become more likely to enroll in affected universities. These results suggest that mass shootings leave institutional and cultural legacies that outlast the students who witnessed them.

That is from the job market paper of María Medellín-Esguerra, who is currently on the job market from Brown University.

The post Do mass shootings in universities lead to permanent effects? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: SemiAnalysis: The Huawei-DeepSeek Symbiosis
item.description:
Original article: https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/huawei-deepseek

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

This summary is based solely on the available text from the newsletter article, which may be a preview.

The publication is SemiAnalysis, the authors are Bryan Shan and Dylan Patel, and the article is titled The Huawei-DeepSeek Symbiosis.

The piece details the mutual dependency forming between DeepSeek and Huawei. DeepSeek possesses cutting-edge artificial intelligence models but lacks hardware access, while Huawei offers hardware and a native software stack through its Ascend platform but needs a frontier lab to prove its chips can handle demanding training and inference. DeepSeek has added Ascend support to multiple repositories, including TileLang, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, FlashMLA, and DeepSelect, signaling an exchange centered around kernel-authoring languages. The authors project that by 2027 or 2028, internal and external pressures will push DeepSeek to rely primarily on Huawei’s stack.

Examining Huawei's hardware, the authors evaluate the Ascend 950PR, which is designed for prefill and recommendation workloads, featuring lower core counts and memory bandwidth than the larger 950DT. Because of manufacturing defects and parametric shortfalls, Huawei bins both compute and high bandwidth memory together across multiple SKUs. Testing an Ascend 950PR SKU with 28 cube cores and 128 gigabytes of high bandwidth memory showed that pointer-chase latency starts at about 134 nanoseconds through 18 blocks, rises to 182 nanoseconds at 56 blocks, and jumps to 391 nanoseconds at 64 blocks, indicating a second wave beyond 56 vector cores.

Each Ascend 950PR also includes Linx816 AArch64 artificial intelligence central processing unit cores, matching middle cores found in the Kirin 9000S and 9010. These embedded central processing units handle scheduling, index selection, gather steps, and key-value metadata to bypass host-to-device communication overhead on short tasks.

In compute microbenchmarks across 1,055 bfloat16 general matrix multiply shapes, stock Huawei kernels hit up to 99.7 percent of their theoretical ceiling. However, on shapes below Ascend’s ridge, Ascend achieved a median of 41.5 percent of attainable performance compared to 46.8 percent for Nvidia’s H100. On absolute numbers, the Ascend 950PR trails modern chips, landing between Nvidia’s A100 and AMD’s MI300X. In memory bandwidth tests, Ascend 950PR exceeded H100 at small message sizes and closely matched it at large sizes, though a mid-curve latency dip occurs when switching to a vector-core TensorMove copy method.

Software co-design bridges this raw hardware gap. TileLang now features a native Ascend 950 backend that handles compilation, synchronization, and memory scheduling, including an AutoSchedule feature that reduces execution time by up to 40 percent on smaller tasks. FlashMLA has been updated to store key-value cache quantized values and scaling factors together, minimizing transfer requests by the memory transfer engine. For multi-rack scale-out communication, DeepEP-Ascend integrates with Ascend supernodes over URMA and Huawei Collective Communication Library, though contention persists between vector operations, combine processing, and memory bandwidth.

An execution profile of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash across 32 Ascend 950DT chips shows heavy use of speculative decoding via DSpark drafter blocks, which significantly accelerates execution compared to full verification passes. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash also incorporates Engram, offloading token input fetching to DRAM to overlap with layer zero computation. In the steady-state window, the primary compute stream occupied 88.8 percent of the duration while contributing 72.6 percent of total device time due to overlapping secondary streams. A theoretical first-order scenario that doubles cube throughput would yield a 1.32-times step improvement.

Finally, the authors note ecosystem challenges. DeepSeek’s custom optimizations prioritize specific supernode and ARM architectures, leaving gaps for standard setups. For instance, current vLLM-Ascend release candidates on x86 hosts suffer from hardcoded ARM headers, broken out-of-the-box startup, lack of DeepGEMM support, and missing continuous integration testing, meaning the symbiosis currently benefits DeepSeek far more than the broader developer ecosystem.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: More on Elizabeth Holmes and prison
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/more-on-elizabeth-holmes-and-prison.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=more-on-elizabeth-holmes-and-prison

The Free Press asked me to expand upon my views of this matter, here is one excerpt from the piece:

Third, fewer women in prison does not have to mean less deterrence overall, as arguably we should concentrate more of our legal resources on deterring violent men. Note that if we can release enough women from prison, more prison space will be freed up, and I mean more prison space for men, including violent men. It is common to read of shortfalls in jail and prison space, which lead to violent men being released early. Many of these men go on to commit violent crimes, a truly major injustice. Or they commit an ongoing string of misdemeanors, sometimes ranging into the dozens or even hundreds, such as shoplifting or disorderly conduct. Our cities become much less livable as a result. If we can, over time, convert some of the current prison space for women into prison space for men, especially violent and destructive men, I expect a net increase of justice in this country. I also think it will be a better country to live in. There is precedent for such a conversion of facilities. In 2013, California turned the Valley State Prison for Women into a men’s prison, as the female prison population was declining and more space was needed to relieve overcrowding among the males. As an economist might say, sending women to prison is not a free lunch. Given that prison space is scarce, it means the release of more violent criminals, mostly male.

Some reliance on prison is unavoidable.  But it amazes me how much people will go to the mat to defend an institution — whole cloth at that — that makes no real sense in terms either humanitarian or even simply organizational.

The post More on Elizabeth Holmes and prison appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/21/ten-minutes-now-two-hundred-minutes-saved/

An idea that we discussed recently that stuck with me: ten extra minutes spent making sure what you send is concise and clear can save the organization two hundred minutes.

The math is simple. Send something vague or sloppy to twenty people, and each of them spends ten minutes decoding what you actually meant.

Brevity and synthesis aren’t just good writing. They’re a form of respect for everyone else’s time.

“First I thought Troilus And Criseyde was the most boring poem in English. Then I thought Beowulf was. Then I thought Paradise Lost was. Now I know that The Faerie Queen is the dullest thing out. Blast it.”
