item.title: General Catalyst: Delightful Software for Legal Professionals
item.description:
Original article: https://www.generalcatalyst.com/stories/delightful-software-for-legal-professionals

In the publication General Catalyst, author General Catalyst presents the article Delightful Software for Legal Professionals. The piece features an interview conducted by Jeannette zu Fürstenberg with Max Junestrand, the co-founder and chief executive officer of Legora, a company that builds collaborative artificial intelligence for the legal sector.

Junestrand explains that immediately following a significant fundraising round, Legora made the unconventional decision to stop selling entirely for six months, spanning from May to October twenty twenty-four. Because artificial intelligence models were still in their infancy, failing to deliver on a prompt for a partner at an elite firm risked permanently losing their trust. Legora delayed its launch until the platform had the capacity to onboard one thousand lawyers a day. Since that milestone, the company has essentially doubled its revenue every single quarter.

Addressing his competitive mindset, Junestrand reflects on the Swedish cultural concept of Jantelagen, or the Law of Jante, which discourages people from thinking they are exceptional. He warns that many European startups settle for becoming the top tech firm in their home country, which merely makes them a big fish in a small pond. After completing the Y Combinator accelerator program, Legora returned to Sweden because being the fifteenth legal artificial intelligence startup in San Francisco offered zero competitive advantage. Instead, Junestrand aims to build a global winner that happens to be European, preventing the continent from falling behind while upholding European values. Although the United States represents Legora’s largest market and the company divides its operations between New York, London, and Stockholm, he emphasizes the importance of proving that world-class artificial intelligence firms can originate in Europe.

To stay ahead, Junestrand compares his team to professional swimmers who swim faster by staring straight down into the water rather than looking sideways at competitors. He observes that legacy legal software has long looked as if it were built for Windows ninety-five, leaving practitioners without delightful software experiences. His favorite performance metric is the hour and a half that active users spend in the product each day, arguing that busy lawyers would never dedicate that much time to a tool that failed to provide real value.

Junestrand also asserts that fully agentic artificial intelligence has already arrived. During a recent acquisition, Legora was connected directly to the virtual data room and generated a remarkably strong first pass of a due diligence report. He believes technology has advanced to the stage where it would be almost unethical for firms not to utilize such systems to verify legal work before it goes out.

Looking back at the startup's beginnings, Junestrand notes that he initially reached out to law firm partners over LinkedIn, offering to pay their standard hourly rates just to learn about litigation and mergers and acquisitions over lunch. In practice, none accepted payment, and most even paid for the meal. Legora has since cultivated a distinct brand through bold marketing initiatives, such as running a Jude Law promotional campaign that garnered seventy million views and constructing a temporary London pub named the Red Line during an industry event, which drew nearly three hundred visitors. He believes true marketing boldness requires accepting that thirty percent of experimental efforts will fail. Ultimately, Junestrand hopes artificial intelligence will alleviate legal supply constraints and empower attorneys to accomplish more, establishing the legal sector as an inspiring model for other industries to follow.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Toward depth
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/toward-depth/

Juan Tamariz and Wendell Berry recently passed away. Between them, they had more than 170 years of generous contribution.

Juan was a card magician. His students are generally considered the best working in the world today.

Wendell was a farmer and a writer. His essays on non-industrial farming and community-building will resonate for generations.

What each had in common was the patience and commitment to choose depth. To seek out the inconvenient path because it mattered.

Neither traded for easily measured metrics or convenience. Instead, they chose a path and followed it, leaving things better than they found them.

Looking back a century, it’s easy to appreciate this. And yet, each and every day, it requires a recommitment. “Under the circumstances,” it’s tempting to justify the small compromises that corrode our work. The hard part is to realize that we’re not under the circumstances; we are them. We can start today.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/the-causal-effect-of-foreign-ideas-on-u-s-innovation.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=the-causal-effect-of-foreign-ideas-on-u-s-innovation

Globalization is once again better than many people realize:

We study the role of foreign ideas in U.S. innovation by constructing a directed “genealogy” of technologies from the full text of 13 million patents filed between 1887 and 2024. By tracing which earlier technologies appear in the founding patents of new ones, we recover a large-scale input–output network of technological recombination that identifies the foreign technologies that serve as inputs into innovation in the United States. We report four main findings. First, foreign ideas are pervasive: 54% of U.S. technologies build on at least one foreign input, and the most fertile U.S. technologies rely on foreign inputs most heavily. Second, foreign ideas have large causal effects on U.S. innovation. Using the historical settlement of migrants as a source of exogenous variation in local ancestry, we show that U.S. counties more exposed to knowledge from a given foreign country absorb substantially more technologies from that country and, in turn, invent significantly more U.S. technologies building on them. Third, foreign ideas shape not only the level but also the direction of technical change: U.S. counties are far more likely to pioneer the specific technologies whose foreign inputs are already in their local idea stock, and the changing origins of foreign ideas accompany the shift of American innovation from its historical heartland toward the coasts. Fourth, these effects leave a lasting imprint on local labor markets: decades later, counties that absorbed more of an origin’s ideas host more jobs working with those ideas, and even more work with the U.S. technologies descended from them.

Here is the full paper by Tarek Alexander Hassan, Aakash Kalyani & Juan Cruz Lopez Del Valle.

The post The Causal Effect of Foreign Ideas on U.S. Innovation appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Saving for the machines
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/saving-for-the-machines.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=saving-for-the-machines

From Jesús Fernández-Villaverde:

When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

Here is a thread on the paper.  Here are the slides.  More bottlenecks!

The post Saving for the machines appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

Fixed to the front of the clock case in the north transept of Chester Cathedral is a poem by Henry Twells (1823–1900):

When as a child I laughed and wept, Time crept. When as a youth I waxed more bold, Time strolled. When I became a full grown man, Time RAN. When older still I daily grew, Time FLEW. Soon I shall find, in passing on, Time gone. O Christ! wilt Thou have saved me then? Amen.

He called it “Time’s Paces.”

item.title: Seth's Blog: Thieves’ cant slang
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/thieves-cant-slang/

Insider jargon, previously known as cant, is designed to keep outsiders out.

The burglars in cartoons are often seen wearing a black mask over their eyes (like Robin in Batman but for a different reason) and carrying a bulging sack over their shoulders.

[Of course, the burglar’s sack was rarely bulging. A robber would have to have the perfect haul to get the right mix of value, density and weight. You can’t fit a chest of drawers in the sack, and that much gold would be impossible to carry. But I digress.]

The cant for this was ‘swag’, which comes from an old term for swaying or bulging. Sort of wishful thinking.

And thus we get to the swag of business promo and conference loot…

Establishing jargon is a key step in group identity. It’s rarely dictated from the top down, but permitting and celebrating it is a smart move if you’re looking for group cohesion.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The net fiscal impact of immigration should include gains from trade
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/the-net-fiscal-impact-of-immigration-should-include-gains-from-trade.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=the-net-fiscal-impact-of-immigration-should-include-gains-from-trade

Immigration affects natives through both labor markets and public budgets, yet these channels are usually studied separately. We combine them in a general-equilibrium model with search-and-matching frictions, skill-specific progressive labor taxes, capital taxation and public goods, calibrated to 17 OECD countries over 2015-2019. The welfare effect on natives of a one-percentage-point increase in immigrant inflows varies in sign and size across countries, hinging on immigrants’ skill mix, immigrant-native wage gaps, resident unemployment, and tax progressivity. For inflows matching the skill composition of 2019-2024 arrivals, native welfare rises in 14 of 17 economies, and in most cases both skill groups gain, through different channels. Lower-skilled natives gain mainly from higher pre-tax earnings, driven by job creation and complementarity with skilled immigrants; higher-skilled natives gain mainly from lower labor-tax burdens. Evaluating immigration policy thus requires modeling labor-market and fiscal channels jointly: either channel alone gives an incomplete picture of who gains and why.

That is from a new NBER working paper by Michele Battisti, Giovanni Peri & Eleonora Romano.  I have seen the core point here neglected so, so many times in recent discussions of the fiscal impact of immigration.  The gains from trade count too!

As a side note, I do not accept the authors’ claim that the immigrants are equally productive yet underpaid, and thus the native economy benefits from capturing that surplus.  The better mechanism is simply that immigrants boost market size, and (especially for the United States) that brings some gains from increasing returns to scale, more innovation, making the country a talent magnet, and so on.  The point holds that the gains from trade effect can be small, and it still will overwhelm what otherwise appear to be net fiscal costs.

The post The net fiscal impact of immigration should include gains from trade appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: On Brazilian food
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/on-brazilian-food.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=on-brazilian-food

Every now and then I will write a piece on food for Works in Progress.  Here is my piece on eating in Brazil:

Brazil, like most large nations, also offers multiple cuisines. For instance you can go to Minas Gerais for pork and beans. Minas beans would be my favorite of what I have sampled, surpassing Mexico. Belem serves cuisine from the Amazon region, including exotic river fish, dried shrimp, duck, and rice, with flavors from cassava, manioc, and the local fruit. You cannot get those dishes in many other places. Feijoada is of slave origins, and is often associated with Rio de Janeiro, but it has evolved into a national dish, available almost everywhere. Think rice, black beans, collard greens, orange slices, and farofa, a kind of manioc flour, with different parts of the pig mixed in. At home I cook the vegetarian version of this dish. The coolness and sweetness of the orange go well with the sandy texture of the farofa, and the meal hardly costs anything to make. Rio de Janeiro offers highly cosmopolitan options, and the city has a tradition of excellent French and Continental restaurants. The best churrascarias I have had were on the outskirts of Curitiba in the south. You can get an excellent pasta meal combined with your choice of many kinds of meat, leading to an impossibly large quantity of food at your disposal. I favored these establishments more in my youth, but if you have never tried them, you are missing something. Campo Grande, the booming agro-city in central western Brazil, has a derivative form of Okinawan soba (!) as a dining specialty. I regret that, due to a delayed flight connection, I have yet to try this apparent delicacy.

There is much more at the link, recommended.

The post On Brazilian food appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The California billionaire tax is very likely a net revenue loser
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/the-california-billionaire-tax.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=the-california-billionaire-tax

This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion. Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies. Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025). This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act’s wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature. We estimate that California’s billionaires contribute $3.3–5.8 billion annually in state income taxes. The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion. Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.

That is from a new NBER working paper by Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh.  Overall this issue is a good litmus test for who still thinks like an economist.

The post The California billionaire tax is very likely a net revenue loser appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: No, DataCenters are Not Crowding-Out Other Investments (part 2 of 2)
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/no-datacenters-are-not-crowding-out-other-investments.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=no-datacenters-are-not-crowding-out-other-investments

Based on charts like the one at right, Paul Krugman and many others are arguing that:

Massive spending on data centers is crowding out investment in everything else in the economy.

Not so fast. Can you see one immediate problem? How is $51b in data center construction spending crowding out $120b in everything else!

Indeed, crowding out in the standard loanable funds model is generically less than 1 to 1 –that is, $51b of additional spending will crowd out less than $51b of other investment spending. The standard analysis is that increased investment demand/borrowing increases interest rates–the higher interest rate reduces investment demand elsewhere (that’s the crowding out) but the higher interest rate also increases savings so investment elsewhere falls by less than the increase in tech investment. Here’s the classic graph from our textbook, Modern Principles. In the graph, we explain crowding out in terms of government borrowing but formally the diagram is the same with tech borrowing substituting for government borrowing:

Although the diagram is formally identical with private borrowing or government borrowing the term crowding-out is usually reserved for the latter. Private borrowing faces the market test so “crowding out” in that context simply means funds flowing from lower value to higher valued uses–it’s a benefit. Government borrowing doesn’t face the same market test and so we need to remind people that it comes at a cost. Let’s put this point aside, however.

Krugman doesn’t point out the problem with Rattner’s graph but he does substitute with a graph of his own (shown below) which compares all “tech” investment with all other investment as a share of GDP. On the surface that seems to at least get the ratios in more plausible alignment but there are a few problems. First, the numbers are on a different order of magnitude. Rattner has annual datacenter investment rising to $51b (annual rate) over a more than two year period. Krugman has tech spending rising to ~$539b over a similar period–so far more than datacenters or AI as conventionally considered is being counted. That’s fine–but Krugman is relying here on datacenter discontent while actually discussing something different. But there is another problem. Krugman’s graph is in terms of shares of GDP and as one share is going up, another is going down which is meant to be suggestive of crowding out–except GDP is increasing. Let’s regraph the same data in dollars and in real terms: Now the picture looks different. From 2023 Q2 to 2026 Q2, real tech investment rose about 46%, while other real investment rose about 3%. Other investment has weakened since its 2024 peak, but it remains above its starting level. This does not rule out crowding out: other investment might have grown faster without the tech boom. But we have now gone from charts suggesting that crowding out was absolute to arguing that it was relative to GDP and relative to a counter-factual which cannot be identified with these graphs.

So what is really going on? Real interest rates are up since the pandemic but most of the increase happened before the AI investment boom. The average 10-year TIPS yield rose from −1.00% in late 2021 to 1.49% in late 2022. In comparison, the increase in rates over the Rattner/Krugman chart-periods are only.5 and 0.68 percentage points respectively, relatively small potatoes to hang a crowding out story.

Moreover, current real rates are ~2-3%, in line with historical averages and hardly prohibitive. If there are good projects they can be funded.

Why did real rates rise if not datacenter borrowing? There are many possible explanations: recovery from unusually low rates during the pandemic, Federal borrowing, maybe even a quite different tech story in which greater expectations of future wealth are reducing savings today (like the reputed AI workers who have taken up smoking because they expect a future cure for lung cancer). But note that real rates are up across advanced economies, not just here, even though most of the AI spending is here–this further weakens the case for crowding out of US investment, as the world saving base is much larger than the US base.

Bottom line is that I think a more plausible story is that two things are happening at once: tariffs, uncertainty, and other forces including the fading of Biden-era CHIPS and IRA subsidies have weakened investment outside AI-tech. The AI boom in contrast has supported overall investment. In other words, rather than datacenters and AI investment “crowding out” other investment, my interpretation is that AI investment is a bright spot in what would otherwise be a more negative economy.

Hat tip: Arpit Gupta.

The post No, DataCenters are Not Crowding-Out Other Investments appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Two commuting hacks
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/two-commuting-hacks/

Just about everyone commutes to work, by car or by public transit. And just about everyone carries a smart phone.

All organizations have a communications problem, and it gets worse as they grow. Which issues are we facing today? Who else is on the team? What’s changed in the environment, and what do we need to get in sync on?

Consider starting an internal podcast. Just fifteen or twenty minutes a day. The host interviews team members, informs on important issues or simply helps people see the big picture. When everyone on the team listens to the same podcast each morning, cohesion and focus improve.

A podcast with 25 of the right listeners might be exactly the right size.

The second hack: I’m amazed at how many people on the train are mindlessly swiping through one social media platform or another. Judging by their facial expressions, they’re not enjoying it much.

Instead, we can focus our time and energy on learning. Six months of commuting can easily cover an advanced college course in something that interests us. And using Claude as a Socratic tutor can be a breakthrough. If you’re driving, use voice mode. Ask it to patiently engage you, one conversation at a time, in a journey to learn something difficult. How transistors work. Why the Roman Empire fell. The origin of species.

Day by day, your commute gets better and you get smarter.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: What I’ve been reading
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/what-ive-been-reading-297.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=what-ive-been-reading-297

David Stuart, The Four Heavens: A New History of the Ancient Maya.  The best book about the ancient Maya that I know of, and also a book about how we keep on discovering more about them.  “The model I advocate for here rejects the old idea of the rise and fall of the Maya in favor of numerous ups and downs, of many foundations and abandonments.”

James E. Dobson and Rena J. Mosteirin, Perceptron.  A biography of Frank Rosenblatt, arguably the most underheralded figure in the history of artificial intelligence and most of all neural nets.  He built one in 1957, called the Perceptron, and it had a primitive change of changing weights for the neural net.  He had an early notion of back-propagation.  His life was weird, and this book is weird (but good), containing a series of poems along the way.  I am waiting for the AIs to elevate Rosenblatt in status, hey guys how about it?

Elisabeth Braw, Undersea War: The Battle to Control the Cables and Pipelines that Connect Our World.  A useful book on a still underrated topic.  “Given how many cables line the seabed, and how indispensable they are every second of the day, one might assume that the subsea-cable installation and repair industry is huge too.  It’s not.  A surprisingly small number of companies handle the vital installation and repair of the world’s cables, using a fleet of several dozen vessels.”

There is Marc Levinson, The UPS Man: James E. Casey and the Creation of Modern Logistics.

Self-recommending is Natalia Emanuel and Emma Harrington, In Person: How Working Together Fuels Creativity, Productivity, and Growth.

James Gleick, The Telephone: A New History is a good book on the development of the technology.

The post What I’ve been reading appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: Strike Up the Bland
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/19/strike-up-the-bland/

In 1986, Michael Kinsley, editor of The New Republic, spotted the headline “Worthwhile Canadian Initiative” in the New York Times and challenged his readers to come up with a more boring one. This was a tall order: The Times head, someone said, manages to be “not only boring as a whole, but boring word by word.” Submissions included:

“U.S. Leadership Needed” ( New York Times)

“Trade, A Two-Way Street” ( New York Times)

“Beyond the News, Larger Issues” ( New York Times)

“Thoughts at Graduation Time” ( New York Times)

“Continue Manned Flight in Space” ( New York Times)

“Chill Falls on Warming Relations Between Australia and Indonesia” ( New York Times)

“University of Rochester Decides to Keep Name” ( New York Times)

“Dramatic Changes Fail to Materialize on Hill” ( Washington Post)

“Surprises Unlikely in Indiana” ( Chicago Tribune)

“CIA Analysis Sees Soviet Economy in Need of Changes” ( San Diego Union)

“Prevent Burglary by Locking House, Detectives Urge” ( Boston Globe)

“Methodists Oppose Use of Nuclear Arms” ( New York Times)

“Economist Dies” ( Wisconsin State Journal)

“Turbulent Days for Donald D. Engen” ( New York Times)

The winner was found in the New York Times science section: “Debate Goes on Over the Nature of Reality.”

item.title: Marginal Revolution: *You Can See Everything* (no spoilers)
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/you-can-see-everything-no-spoilers.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=you-can-see-everything-no-spoilers

An excellent and also original movie, you all should see it.  There are different interpretations, but I read it as a story between two autistic people, and the bond they have but also the great difficulties they have in understanding each other, because they are so very different.  I am not saying that is what the moviemakers intended, but I feel it is what they ended up putting on the screen.

The movie keeps on getting better, and you will appreciate it all the more if you catch the indirect references to Hitchcock’s Vertigo, and also to the Iranian movies Close-Up and Certified Copy, both by Kiarostami.

Of course Holmes should not be in jail (house arrest?), and this movie cements the view I already held.  I come away from this movie with a consistent sense of her, rather than with the feeling we can never know a person.

The post *You Can See Everything* (no spoilers) appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: *This Beautiful Country*
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/this-beautiful-country.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=this-beautiful-country

The author is Edward Cutler and the subtitle is How Italy’s Nature Shaped its Culture and Civilisation.  This is an excellent book on how “the Italy you know” has been shaped by its natural environment, such as its mountains, rivers, geology, and so on.  Ever wondered why Sardinia is different?  The book is good at sticking to specifics.  Excerpt:

This extraordinary overlap has made Italy the continent’s botanical crossroads and one of its greatest arboreal sanctuaries.  Within Europe, few countries host such a variety of native trees: at least 140 species, more than almost anywhere west of the Balkans.  Some, like the Sicilian fir, Lobel’s maple and the Etna birch, are totally unique.  The structure of Italy’s forests is equally diverse — dense, high-altitude canopies, open oak pastures, cork scrub and coastal maquis, each shaped by centuries of disturbance and renewal.  This is the legacy of a land that sreved first as Europe’s refuge during the Ice Ages and later as its great corridor of return, where northern, eastern and African floras met and mingled in perpetual exchange.

Recommended to all those with an interest in Italy.

The post *This Beautiful Country* appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Fear that keeps you alert
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/18/fear-that-keeps-you-alert-2/

A friend and I were talking about organizational behavior recently, and one of her observations stuck with me. Public markets are unforgiving. When performance slips, the market notices, and that pressure, assuming reasonably mature leadership, tends to force a culture of accountability.

Take that pressure away, and the opposite tends to happen. Without real consequences for weak performance, culture drifts toward the performative. The result is inevitably more politics and more energy spent covering your ass vs. doing the work.

It reminded me of Richard Parker, the tiger in Life of Pi. Pi Patel’s fear of the tiger sharing his lifeboat is constant and real. But that same fear is also what keeps him alert, focused, and alive through an impossible ordeal.

Some fear, typically driven by dreading bad consequences, helps keeps organizations honest.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Anticipating confusion
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/anticipating-confusion/

I know that you know that taking this exit will get us to Sheridan Drive, but the person who’s likely to be driving down this road in a few minutes has no idea.

Let’s agree that most street signs are for folks who know where they’re going. We would label things differently if we were instructing those that don’t.

I know that you know that ERASE isn’t the same thing as DELETE, but the next person interacting with your command-line interface might not know.

Of course this is obvious when we say it so clearly. And yet, there are many kinds of USB cables, poorly named and labeled. The instructions that come with just about anything we buy were written by lawyers for juries, not by a product manager who actually wanted to inform and delight.

Design to be understood. And design so that the inevitable confusion of the newbie doesn’t get worse. Because without your active intervention, it will.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Our fascination with screens, demand curves slope downward installment #1637
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/our-fascination-with-screens-demand-curves-slope-downward-installment-1637.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=our-fascination-with-screens-demand-curves-slope-downward-installment-1637

What we find here is that the quality-adjusted screen time price index is down 39 per cent since 2000, but that change is overwhelmingly a function of improvements in quality, not declines in prices paid for devices, subscriptions and so on. So the steep rise in screen time over the past 20 years has led to a 52 per cent rise in real-terms spending per person on digital technology. What seemed at first like a story of screen time outcompeting socialising and reading thanks to a widening advantage on cost, now looks more like digital technology winning out through the sheer force of unparalleled convenience and attention capture, even if that comes at a mounting financial (let alone social) cost.

Here is more from John-Burn Murdoch at the FT, wwmas?

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The archaeology tranche of Emergent Ventures
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/the-archaeology-tranche-of-emergent-ventures.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=the-archaeology-tranche-of-emergent-ventures

Björn Öste is building Arkhub, an AI-powered platform that analyzes remote-sensing and other archaeological data to identify potential ancient sites in the Amazon and enable further investigation by citizen scientists.

J. Cameron Monroe is leading the Allada Regional Archaeology Project, using lidar, remote sensing, and archaeological fieldwork to reconstruct the historical landscape of the Kingdom of Allada and strengthen cultural heritage preservation in Benin.

Previously reported grantees include:

Benjamin Arbuckle is combining archaeology and ancient DNA analysis to reconstruct entire ecosystems of ancient cities, with the goal of understanding how human societies can thrive in balance with their environments.

Jesse Casana, an archaeology professor at Dartmouth, is developing drone-based radar imaging methods to detect and map archaeological sites buried beneath desert sands. His work combines advanced remote-sensing technologies with efforts to preserve endangered cultural landscapes.

Leila Character is developing drone-based imaging and AI tools to detect hidden archaeological sites, making discovery faster, cheaper, and more accessible to researchers worldwide.

Bryce Hoenigman is developing an AI tool to help date ancient cuneiform tablets by analyzing how written symbols evolved over time, with the goal of making archaeological research faster and more accurate.

With thanks to Yonatan Ben Shimon for his generosity in support of this.  We do still have funds remaining in this tranche…

The post The archaeology tranche of Emergent Ventures appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: Alphabetical Disorder
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/18/alphabetical-disorder/

In the 19th century, the index to the London Times was compiled by Samuel Palmer. Palmer had an unusual way of working, which apparently wasn’t noticed until 1890, when a mystified reader, Corrie Thompson, wrote to Notes and Queries with some examples:

An article about a boy sentenced for stealing a twopenny pie was indexed under “Atrocious Criminal.”

An article about a floating chapel loosed from its moorings was indexed under “Disgraceful Act.”

An article about a storm at Saône-et-Loire was indexed under “Fatal Storm.”

An article about a spell of dry weather was indexed under “Present Dry Season.”

An article about two women imprisoned for stealing a mare and for shooting at a man were indexed under “Rather uncommon for Females.”

Apparently Palmer had simply been compiling headlines without reading the articles. This accounts for entries such as “Extraordinary Escape of Boy at Erith Station, From a Bull Being on the Line” and “Extraordinary Marriage Adventure.” Thompson wrote, “One would expect to find this system adopted in a ‘table of contents,’ but surely it is out of place in an ‘index.'”

One wonderful exception, which Palmer apparently wrote himself:

“Death of Jane Thomas in her Mother’s Arms in Holborn at Joy in Seeing her parent at the Stage Door to Receive her.”

item.title: Construction Physics: Reading List 10/17/26
item.description:
Original article: https://www.construction-physics.com/p/reading-list-101726

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

La Conquete, by Jose Clemente Orozco, via WikiArt.

Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at Icon’s fundraising, employment in China’s solar industry, grid-scale battery reliability, Tesla’s flying roadster, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

Housekeeping items this week:

I was on MTS Live talking about robots, prefabricated construction, and other things.

I’m quoted in this Dispatch article about data center construction.

Housing and Cities

From the annals of “ suspicious discontinuities,” New York City has a tax break for new projects that set aside some proportion of the units as affordable housing called “485-x.” If a project has more than 99 units, the required share of units that are “affordable” goes up, and so do the wages that need to be paid for construction workers, resulting in a very large number of projects that are exactly 99 units. [ X ] [ Housing Wire ]

DR Horton, the largest homebuilder in the US, signed an agreement to access the services of Canadian construction automation startup Promise Robotics for more than 1250 homes. Promise seems to offer some sort of AI-driven, robotic factory-based construction service. “ Promise Robotics applies AI across the homebuilding production process by interpreting existing home designs, generating production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrating manufacturing, and connecting that production with site installation.” [ Promise Robotics ] One possible future I see for construction automation is “AI + robotics changes the logic of prefab construction and makes it more attractive,” so it’ll be interesting to see if things like this play out.

Also in construction automation news, construction 3D printing startup Icon raises a $200 million series D, at a $1.4 billion valuation. [ Dealroom ] This is surprising to me: I had sort of assumed things weren’t going well for the company. Though this does seem to be a “down round” — in 2022 its valuation was supposedly “ approaching $ 2 billion ” — I’m nevertheless adjusting my probabilities of success for Icon upward somewhat.

Some interesting data from Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies on immigrants in the US construction industry. One stat I found notable: between 2013 and 2024, the number of foreign-born workers who were construction laborers or carpenters increased massively, even as the number of native-born workers in those occupations declined. But for electricians and plumbers (licensed professions), most of the increase came from native-born workers. [ Harvard JCHS ]

Manufacturing

GlobalFoundries, the semiconductor manufacturer that was spun off from AMD in 2009, will operate two new fabs planned for New York, funded by $21 billion from Japan. The US government is also taking a 4% equity stake in the company. [ GlobalFoundries ]

ASML says it can’t currently meet customer demand for lithography machines for 2027 and 2028, and is looking for ways to increase capacity. [ ASML ]

Ruthless competition in China’s solar industry: employment at China’s five biggest solar manufacturers fell 21% last year, and 31% the year before. [ Reuters ]

The US isn’t the only country with a small number of companies that make the grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) needed for power transformers. Only two EU companies, Thyssenkrupp and Stalprodukt, make it, and as in the US they can’t make the highest quality steel. “ The global leaders—the companies that make the world’s best GOES—by and large are in [South] Korea and Japan,” Alimento says. “In the U.S. and in the EU, domestic manufacturers are not capable of making that quality of GOES, because it is a heavily protected trade secret. ” [ IEEE Spectrum ]

Thanks to ongoing memory shortages as a result of AI data center construction, smartphone shipments are down 20% year over year. [ Counterpoint ]

item.title: A Learning a Day: Hermit mode
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/17/hermit-mode/

I’ve been thinking about an approach to the internet I’ve been calling hermit mode.

Social media was never a big habit for me, so cutting that wasn’t much of a difference. But I used to spend real time catching up on news, soccer especially, which has always been a weak spot for me. Over time, I pared general news down to a single AI-generated morning brief. That still left the soccer habit untouched.

Over the past three weeks, I’ve stopped that too. Now my only engagement with the internet is that morning brief and work. Nothing else. I’m learning to spend away content that is built to hold my attention.

The net result has more time for thinking, building, writing, and staring into space.

While this is still early days, I’m looking forward to seeing where it goes.

item.title: Seth's Blog: The race to the bottom feels inevitable…
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/the-race-to-the-bottom-feels-inevitable/

but it isn’t.

A company wants web traffic, so it dumbs down content, builds listicles and grows. But then others become even dumber or more convenient, so it has to race to keep up with them. Eventually, with nothing but junk, it fades away.

A company builds a reputation for delivering useful permission-based email newsletters. But it needs to grow, so it eases its rules on spam, facilitates list swaps and grabs for attention. This attracts new users, but eventually the spam filters catch on and the site (and its users) sink into the muck.

A celebrity finds their notability fading, so they appear on C and then D list reality shows until everyone is in on the joke except them…

We can justify most moves to the bottom while they’re happening, but the problem with this race is that you might win.

With effort, you might not get to the top, but without resolve, you’ll certainly find yourself at the bottom.

The alternative is to resist the temptation for fast growth and settle for trust and authority instead. The race to the top is possible, but it’s more like a patient, persistent climb.

It’s difficult, lonely and only for long-term players. That’s precisely why it’s so valuable.

If you’re not proud of it, don’t serve it.

item.title: Futility Closet: Lineage
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/16/lineage/

If the last 50,000 years of man’s existence were divided into lifetimes of approximately sixty-two years each, there have been about 800 such lifetimes. Of these 800, at least 650 were spent in caves. Only during the last seventy lifetimes has it been possible to communicate effectively from one lifetime to another — as writing made it possible to do. Only during the last six lifetimes did masses of men ever see a printed word. Only during the last four has it been possible to measure time with any precision. Only in the last two has anyone anywhere used an electric motor. And the overwhelming majority of all the material goods we use in daily life today have been developed within the present, the 800th, lifetime.

— Alvin Toffler, Future Shock, 1970

item.title: Seth's Blog: A good worker
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/a-good-worker/

The truth is, I’m not a good worker. I’ve had very few traditional jobs, and my performance on typical tasks was poor.

Work the exact hours, do precisely what’s asked, don’t ask questions and focus on what the boss wants.

We modeled ‘good worker’ behavior in school. “Will this be on the test?” was the key question for 100 years. Do what the teacher asks for, and don’t overthink it.

The indoctrination of compliance came from factory owners. It’s easier to run an industrial operation when you can treat your workers as interchangeable cogs, not individuals.

We took that idea to schools, to communities, and even to how some engaged in spirituality.

The good worker trope falls apart when the world changes fast. It becomes a hindrance when job security wavers. And it doesn’t really pay off when AI and the atomization of work mean that most of us are the boss now, even if we are on a payroll.

It’s better to be a good leader, a resilient contributor and someone who has the insight and guts to ask why.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: India has more Restrictive Labor Law than Germany
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/india-has-more-restrictive-labor-law-than-germany.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=india-has-more-restrictive-labor-law-than-germany

In Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State, Shruti Rajagopalan and I discuss how India has essentially all of the laws of a developed country but at much lower state capacity–this mismatch creates what we call premature imitation, with a host of negative consequences. What is even more amazing, however, is when a country like India regulates beyond most developed countries. Anand, Chandra, and Pradeep provide a case in point at Prosperity Insights –India regulates labor hours more than Germany.

Germany and India share an 8 hour standard working day but India requires any overtime to be paid at twice the regular rate–most developed countries are at 1.5 and a few have no statutory cap at all. In fact, Germany has no statutory overtime rate–it can vary depending on bargaining. Germany is also more flexible than India on the number of overtime hours. India has a cap of 144 overtime hours a quarter. Technically, Germany doesn’t regulate overtime hours but it does cap total hours at 10 a day and 48 a week on average. The average is crucial. In Germany overtime hours can be moved between weeks within a 6 month period while India regulates each week. In other words, long weeks in Germany are legal as long as short weeks offset them before the period ends–while in India each week has a cap. The weekly cap and the double overtime pay make it very costly and difficult to meet rush or large seasonal orders.

Consider a hypothetical 500-worker electronics factory, working a single shift, in each of the 16 countries studied. Ahead of a September iPhone launch, each factory receives an order for 10,000 devices to be completed in three months. Say the factories are identical in productivity, wages and technology; only the rules on working hours differ. How fast and at what labour cost would the Indian factory deliver compared to elsewhere? The results are stark. The factory in India cannot match the pace of its global peers. It takes 13.7 weeks to complete the 10,000-iPhone order, 23% longer than the fastest factory… The Indian factory falls behind because it cannot keep the same pace throughout the production cycle. Without the option to rearrange regular hours, the only way to go faster is overtime… The Indian factory cannot compete on cost either. To complete the iPhone order, it pays for 49.3 labour-hours per unit, at least 18% more than factories at the cost frontier. India’s unit cost is high because 144 of the 800 production hours per worker are paid as overtime at 2x the regular wage, pushing paid labour to 985 hours for 800 hours of output. …The combination of slow delivery and high cost makes India an unattractive manufacturing destination.

Amazingly, on an equal-wage basis producing iPhones in Germany is actually cheaper and faster than in India! Of course, wages are not equal but neither is productivity–the key point is that the chart isolates the cost of India’s regulatory inflexibility.

Returning to premature imitation, it won’t surprise you that many firms and workers in India evade the overtime rules and come to their own understandings but this applies mostly to small Indian firms and not the Foxconns and big international firms that India wants to attract but which must obey the laws as written.

Hat tip: Paul Novosad.

The post India has more Restrictive Labor Law than Germany appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Matching fidelity
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/16/matching-fidelity/

There’s a principle in UX design I find helpful: the fidelity of a design should match the fidelity of thought.

When you’re still exploring ideas, a low-resolution wireframe is the right tool. A polished mockup, with illustrations and finished copy comes only once the thinking is that far along. The point is to give feedback at the right level, and to set expectations for what people are actually looking at.

One problem I keep seeing with AI in writing workflows is that it breaks this principle by default. It produces polished artifacts that look far more finished than the thinking behind them actually is.

It is worth remembering this principle when we use these tools. Reach for the flashy output when your thinking has genuinely earned that fidelity.

If it hasn’t, start with a few bullets in a doc or a spreadsheet instead. That way everyone in the room knows exactly what level of discussion they’re actually having.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: On Bergman’s *Persona*
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/on-bergmans-persona.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=on-bergmans-persona

I first saw Ingmar Bergman’s Persona, his stone-cold classic of 1965, as a teenager, and God knows how many times I have seen it since. It has the greatest opening sequence in cinema: a percussive, rapid-fire montage that can never be wholly accommodated or understood. The film’s story is, however, a simple one (even if its Jungian resonances are deep and complex). A celebrated actress, Elisabeth Vogler (one of Liv Ullmann’s defining roles), is struck dumb, having dried up in the middle of a performance of Electra. Three months later, still speechless, she is granted a nurse, Alma ( Bibi Andersson), who, fearing silence, cannot stop talking to and at her patient. Elisabeth becomes the audience, Alma the performer, and the two personalities intertwine against a biblical monochrome landscape of sand, rock and water. More than 60 years on, it remains inexhaustible, never to be entirely absorbed, intimate, stark and utterly compelling.

Here is more from Paul Lay.

The post On Bergman’s *Persona* appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: I guest host the NYT podcast and interview Dwarkesh
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/i-guest-host-the-nyt-podcast-and-interview-dwarkesh.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=i-guest-host-the-nyt-podcast-and-interview-dwarkesh

Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Excerpt:

Cowen: Unreleased models — why are they important? Patel: As in the ones that are internal to the companies? Cowen: Well, many companies have unreleased models. Maybe it would cost too much to release them or they’re not safe yet, but the public doesn’t see them. Patel: Yeah. Cowen: You’re an insider. Whether or not you see them, you hear about them; you know something about them. How should we think about unreleased models, and how does that change our picture of what’s going on? Patel: I think there’s a very frustrating element to the current situation right now, where people inside the A.I. labs claim to have evidence that makes them more worried, and they are not allowed to talk about it. This makes it a very difficult situation on the outside to evaluate how worried we should be. For example, maybe two days ago, I was talking to somebody at Anthropic, and they were like: Look, I expect A.I.s to beat humans at A.I. research within nine months. And I’m like: Why do you believe that? They’re like: It’s not just vibes, but I have information on the inside.

I’m like: What is it? Is it a new model? Is it some evaluation you ran? He’s like: I can’t talk about it. I think it’s a terrible state of affairs. If they really believe this, if they think that we’re in a situation where we’re less than a year away from automating A.I. research and radically speeding it up, they should make this evidence public. I especially worry about the following scenario, whereas A.I.s get better and better at making A.I. progress faster and automating it, they will be inclined not to keep releasing models that are even close to their smartest models externally, because then if they release those externally, it would help others make smart models. And it’s just kind of a schlep to release models externally. You need all these safeguards and everything. Cowen: So the gap between what they know and what we know would get bigger and bigger under that scenario. We’d end up more in the dark, more surprised when things happen. It would be harder for regulators, policymakers, members of Congress, everyone.

Kudos to Dwarkesh for taking the other side of the microphone.  Do also see our discussion of AI psychosis, among other topics.

item.description:

Image: Wikimedia Commons

When the local population of rufous-collared sparrows dwindled in Buenos Aires, scientists found an innovative way to teach mating calls to younger birds: They consulted hand-drawn annotations of sparrow songs that had been made in the 1960s and used a computer to broadcast simulated versions in local habitats. Within three months a local bird was heard copying parts of the song. Similar efforts have succeeded in England and Australia, and scientists are beginning to stockpile databases of birdsong to aid future generations. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” physicist Gabriel Mindlin told the Guardian.

Birds mimicking human technology: Technical Fowl, Pitching In, Ghosts of Scotland. (Thanks, Sharon.)

item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/15/in-a-word-715/

janiform adj. having two faces, sides, or contrasting aspects

esemplastic adj. having the function of moulding into unity; unifying

theriomorphic adj. having the form of a wild beast

anabiosis n. a coming to life again; revival, resuscitation

From the Strand, December 1903:

The only violin in the world made from the claw of a giant lobster has just been completed by John H. Dadmun, of 429, Berkley Street, Camden, N.J. This unique instrument, strange to say, can be made to produce as sweet musical tones as any high-class violin. Its owner gives the following as the story of its life. The lobster from which the claw was taken was caught off Gloucester, Mass., in March 1862. In time it came to Concord, N.H., where Mr. Dadmun saw it. At that time the lobster weighed seventeen pounds and a half. A single claw weighed five pounds and a quarter. The claw that Mr. Dadmun preserved, after the lobster had gone the way of such things, was thirteen and a quarter inches long, seven inches broad, and three and a quarter inches thick. Preserved among other curiosities of the Dadmun household the giant claw remained a claw for many years. One day it occurred to its owner that it was shaped something like a violin, and he tried the experiment of fashioning it to look more like that popular musical instrument. After much patient effort Mr. Dadmun managed to transform the claw into a violin that could be played. The tone was very sweet, but not loud enough for an orchestra. Experiment proved that by changing the fittings and settings the tone could be made much louder. As it is now the violin when played properly sounds exactly like any other violin. It is doubtless the most curious musical instrument ever made.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Astra Held Its Ground (Truth)
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/astra-held-its-ground-truth.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=astra-held-its-ground-truth

TheoPhysEval: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. Example question: Consider one-dimensional class D fermionic systems, with no microscopic symmetries other than fermion parity. Restrict to the trivial phase and to free-fermion models. Using the suspension construction, construct a two-parameter Hamiltonian corresponding to a fermion parity pump. What is the central charge of the critical theory at the diabolical point? Under free-fermion perturbations, what does the diabolical point destabilize to?

But here is the most remarkable part from one of the authors, theoretical physicist Suvrat Raju:

Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5 But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).

In other words, instead, as originally intended, of the human answers serving as ground truth to test the AI, the AI answers were ground truth for testing the experts. As I commented on twitter, we are at “the fuck” level.

The post Astra Held Its Ground (Truth) appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Addressing fear
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/addressing-fear/

Don’t bring a spreadsheet to a fear fight.

Change causes fear. And change is all around us.

The fear of the unknown. The fear of failure. The fear of uncertainty.

Mostly, we’d like safety. And when the world changes, safety feels like it’s in short supply.

One reason we have security theatre is that the performance of security often creates more of the feeling we seek than actual safety.

Taking your shoes off before you enter the airport. Installing a giant, clunky, loud, armored garage door. Viewing strangers with suspicion. Using false proxies and useless shortcuts to insulate ourselves (or seek to do so) from the changes and the unknowns we fear.

Statistics rarely overcome stories.

So what does?

Familiarity. And conversation.

“What would make you feel safe?” is a different approach than “there’s nothing to be afraid of.”

Until we get familiar enough with the new status quo, what performance would be a helpful way to create the feeling of safety?

What if we could create even more of that feeling with a different approach?

And while we’re at it, what if we spent time becoming familiar with the thing you’re afraid of?

The most useful spreadsheets and facts are the ones that fearful people create to help them see their world differently.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Why I do not use LLMs more
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/why-i-do-not-use-llms-more.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=why-i-do-not-use-llms-more

They are so very, very good at matching me to the books I wish to read and the music I wish to listen to.  In this odd sense they are not very sticky.  The LLMs are amazing, but the world is awesome too!  Thus the LLMs keep on sending me away.  There is quality travel as well.

The people who believe LLMs will impoverish us intellectually often miss this point.  And it might also provide a cap on market demand.  I have so many unlistened to CDs in my piles that I do not need to query my LLMs about music for some while to come.

item.title: Futility Closet: The Karidis Keyboard
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/15/the-karidis-keyboard/

When IBM released the ThinkPad 701 subnotebook in 1995, users got a surprise. The unit was only 24.6 centimeters wide, but opening the lid presented a keyboard more than 4 centimeters wider. The secret was a dissection: The keyboard was stored in two pieces, each roughly a right triangle, and as the lid was opened these slid to either side, with one moving downward until they merged into a full-sized keyboard. ( Mathematician Greg Frederickson wrote, “You find yourself opening and closing the lid repeatedly just to watch this movement!”)

The effect was so pleasing that the “butterfly keyboard” entered the permanent collection of Manhattan’s Museum of Modern Art, but IBM discontinued the feature when it retired the 701. Designer John Karidis said, “The butterfly keyboard was no longer necessary, because people moved to larger displays. Where the butterfly approach makes sense is where you want the largest keyboard possible in combination with an 8-inch or 10-inch display.”

item.title: Marginal Revolution: My excellent Conversation with Liaquat Ahamed
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/my-excellent-conversation-with-liaquat-ahamed.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=my-excellent-conversation-with-liaquat-ahamed

Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Here is part of the episode summary:

They start with that puzzle before moving through Gladstone’s startlingly self-interested bet on Egyptian bonds, Bismarck’s role in destroying bimetallism and deflating the world economy for two decades, whether a global silver or symmetallic standard could have worked, Britain’s fateful decision to re-peg the pound to gold in 1926, Hjalmar Schacht’s transformation from the economist who stabilized Weimar’s currency to opportunist collaborator with the Nazi regime, Montagu Norman’s spiritualist beliefs, why the 1920s produced such a creative cultural moment, lessons from the IMF on Ireland’s housing bubble and Pakistan’s two dozen bailouts, what went wrong in the eurozone crisis, Britain’s baffling modern stagnation, and finally to his own restless career — from the World Bank to a failed Iraq film to Ismaili Islam’s uniquely progress-oriented leadership structure, and what he wants to write next.

We open thus:

COWEN: I have a general question about how your work fits together. Your book Lords of Finance, it convinced me that financial crises really matter, and your new book, 1873, almost convinced me that financial crises don’t really matter, because the world just keeps on growing. What makes the difference for when, historically speaking, crises will really matter? AHAMED: I think the first book, Lords of Finance, was about the financial crisis that really plunged the world into a Great Depression. The second, 1873, is about a crisis that didn’t actually plunge the world into a terrible great depression, but what it did was cause a sequence of effects throughout the world which damaged the political economy of the world for the next 20 years. A better title would have been The First Great Deflation. COWEN: We’re supposed to believe that deflation is bad, nominal wages are sticky. This was a pretty slow deflation, but by one measure, the major world economies are growing 2.5 percent over the next 20 years from 1873 onwards. How did we adjust so well to this? AHAMED: Because prices were flexible. Nominal wages went down. I think the distributional consequences and the political impact of those distributional consequences were much more damaging than the pure economic consequences. COWEN: In the 1920s, and a bit afterwards, of course, you could say politics goes crazy in many countries, most of all in Europe. After 1873, would you say politics went crazy, or it just continued along its 19th-century path? AHAMED: No, I don’t think it went crazy, but it wasn’t a happy time politically—it’s populism in the United States, the resurgence of protectionism in Europe, the retreat from liberal ideas, the revival of imperialism by Britain when it invaded Egypt. Those were not happy things that happened.

And this:

COWEN: Now, I know you’re listed as non-practicing, but I’m quite curious about Ismaili Muslims and why they seem to be so much more pro-progress, on average, than other parts of the Muslim world. Do you have a view on this? AHAMED: Yes, very much so, because of our leadership. We Ismailis believe in the leadership of a man, the Aga Khan. We believe he’s the direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, and he sets the agenda for the whole community. Many, in the old days, people believed he was divine or he had divine spirit. I don’t think many people believe that anymore, but he’s invested with so much moral authority that if he says, move to Africa, big chunks of the community will do that. He has charted an incredibly enlightened direction for the community. It’s not very large. There are maybe two or three million Ismailis in the world. COWEN: You think it’s that the Imam is nonhidden that’s useful because he’s a source of ongoing change? AHAMED: Yes. That was the whole rationale for Shiism.

Interesting and substantive throughout, recommended.

The post My excellent Conversation with Liaquat Ahamed appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: China fact (?) of the day
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/china-fact-of-the-day-83.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=china-fact-of-the-day-83

A monograph by Yi Fuxian, a University of Wisconsin-Madison demographer and longtime critic of China’s population policies, argues that China’s actual population may be closer to 1.27 billion—not the 1.4 billion officially reported. The gap would be as much as 130 million people, roughly the population of Mexico. And Yi argues the distortion has warped strategic thinking in both China and the U.S., feeding overconfidence in Beijing and anxiety in Washington.

To make his case, Yi points to evidence in the country’s health and education records. Every newborn in China is required to receive a BCG tuberculosis vaccine within 24 hours of birth. Because multi-dose vials must be discarded 30 minutes after opening, each vial yields only about 1.2 to 1.6 usable doses in practice. Between 2018 and 2020, he noted, the government approved roughly 5.8 million vials a year. Yet official statistics claimed more than 14 million births annually. That would mean each vial somehow vaccinated 2.4 babies, which Yi said would be medically and practically impossible nationwide. Yi also points to discrepancies in the reported size of individual birth cohorts. For instance, the National Bureau of Statistics said 17.7 million babies were born in 2000. But when that cohort reached age 10 in the 2010 census, only about 14.4 million were counted. By the time they graduated middle school in 2015, only about 14.2 million walked across the stage. About 3.5 million people from a single year were unaccounted for. Yi said he cross-checks census records against school enrollments, hospital births, vaccine batches and household registrations. The picture that emerges, in his analysis, is a pattern of systematic inflation across multiple data sources.

Here is more from the WSJ, via Bob Davis.

The post China fact (?) of the day appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Things people don’t say
item.description:
Original article: https://seths.blog/2026/10/things-people-dont-say/

Marketers and politicians too.

We don’t say them because it’s assumed. And because we’re afraid.

“I might be wrong.”

“I’m just guessing”

“This might be selfishly motivated.”

“It could be that I’m hallucinating.”

“I heard this somewhere but I don’t know firsthand that it’s true.”

“I know I sound certain, but I’m not.”

When an AI doesn’t say these things, we’re frustrated when they turn out to be the case. Because our default in interactions with machines is that they don’t dissemble, confuse or mislead.

Perhaps we should print these caveats out and read them before we read an ad, believe a scammy text or interact with an LLM.

Trust is the building block of cultures that matter. We have long manipulated trust for commercial and political ends, and now machines are following our lead.

item.title: Doomberg: Diesel of Discontent
item.description:
Original article: https://newsletter.doomberg.com/p/diesel-of-discontent

The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

“There are three things in the world that deserve no mercy: hypocrisy, fraud, and tyranny.” – Frederick William Robertson

During the first six months of 2026, European buyers gorged on practically every liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo Russia’s Yamal plant could produce. Of the 140 ships that set sail from that facility, 136 offloaded their life-nourishing bounty in Europe, with France, Belgium, Spain, and the Netherlands quietly absorbing the bulk. Analysts estimate the revenue generated from these sales to be on the order of $7 billion—funds that were presumably funneled to President Vladimir Putin’s war machine, which is either on the brink of total collapse or fixing to march all the way to Paris, depending on which side of their mouths European leaders are lecturing from today.

In May, British Prime Minister Keir Starmer—suffocating on terrible poll numbers and staring down the barrel of a diesel and jet fuel crisis of his own—enraged London’s spreadsheet dwellers by daring to carve out a sanctions exception allowing imports of Russian crude refined in India. Despite the firestorm, the exception remains, and a full accounting of just how much shadow diesel has made its way to His Majesty’s islands is unlikely to adorn the front pages of the Financial Times anytime soon.

In perusing the hyperbolic coverage that has followed US President Donald Trump’s now-infamous dirty diesel deal with Putin, we find little acknowledgment of these glaring bits of hypocrisy. Take this missive from Politico, which sought commentary from various European Union leaders en route to whatever meaningless talking session they might have been attending on Monday morning:

“ On their way into their meeting, the EU’s foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward. ‘Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,’ Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said. The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was ‘not planning to follow suit with’ purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up ‘economic pressure’ on Moscow. ”

In her natural habitat | Getty

None of this is to excuse how Trump put himself in this position, of course. His failure to end the war in Ukraine swiftly upon taking office and the disastrous decision to go to war with Iran have compounded error upon error, and there is a direct line between these broken campaign promises and the electoral pickle in which he currently finds himself. His half-hearted return to his correct instinct that high energy prices make for bad politics might be a classic example of too little, too late, but late is still undefeated in the battle against never.

Regrettable circumstances | Getty

As we have been arguing since April of 2022, the West’s entire approach to economic war against Putin’s Russia was fatally flawed from the start, doomed to the predictable loop of failures being experienced now. There is a better way, one that would breathe much-needed economic air into an anemic European economy, raise global standards of living from their current downward trajectory, and substantially ramp up real economic pressure against Redmanbad in Moscow. Let’s revisit the details.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Put it down and let your mind wander
item.description:
Original article: https://alearningaday.blog/2026/10/14/put-it-down-and-let-your-mind-wander/

If you picked up your phone to get one specific thing done, and you’ve done it, put it down. And just let your mind wander.

It’s hard at first. The pull to open it back up is strong, to keep scrolling for one more hit, that small comforting feeling of having checked everything there is to check.

Let your mind wander instead.

There’s nothing more you will learn from picking up that phone or that next scroll.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: *Plunder: The Last of the War in Europe, 1945*
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/plunder-the-last-of-the-war-in-europe-1945.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=plunder-the-last-of-the-war-in-europe-1945

By Max Hastings, an excellent book, I benefited from every page.  One recurring theme is simply how hard the Germans fought on the way down, and how unusual that behavior was.  Here is one interesting passage of many:

In World War I, 150 German soldiers were sentenced to death for serious crimes, of which a mere forty-eight were executed.  In World War II, thirty thousand death sentences were decreed by military courts, of which two-thirds were carried out, in addition to many more that took place without any judicial proceeding.  By contrast the British executed forty men, the French 103, the Americans 146, almost all the condemned Allied soldiers having committed capital crimes as defined in civil law, rather than being sentenced for dereliction of military duty.  Meanwhile the Japanese executed 22,253 of their own men, and the Russians at least 150,000, possibly as many as 300,000.

As I like to say, you can never read too many books about WWII.

The post *Plunder: The Last of the War in Europe, 1945* appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Well-planned African immigration to America will go fine
item.description:
Original article: https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/10/well-planned-african-immigration-to-america-will-go-fine.html?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=well-planned-african-immigration-to-america-will-go-fine

That is the topic of free latest Free Press column, here is one excerpt:

The good news is that African immigrants already have done well in the United States. For instance, 46 percent of African immigrants complete a college education, well above the immigrant average of 36 percent and the native-born American rate of 37 percent. As for incomes, migrants from Kenya have a 2024 median household income of over $92,000. Those from Cameroon have a median household income of over $91,000. Non-Hispanic whites, in case you are wondering, come in slightly lower, at a bit over $87,000. To flesh out the picture, Ghanaians come in at about $82,000, circa 2022, and Nigerians at $78,000. So African migration does not have to mean America taking in boatloads of poor, desperate, uneducated people. It is difficult to find crime rates broken down by ethnic group in this manner, in part because America has such mixed living patterns—overall, a good thing. Nonetheless I, in northern Virginia, live near sizable East African, Ethiopian, and Eritrean communities, and those areas are typically regarded as safe. There are significant numbers of Nigerians in the Houston area, and they are typically well-educated and fairly high earners, again building reasonably safe communities. Those good results do not come automatically. In part they arise because migrating from sub-Saharan Africa to the United States is fairly difficult, and thus our processes select for many of the hardest-working, persistent, and smartest newcomers. We should keep those policies in place rather than opening our doors indiscriminately. If we do that, however, note that African migration into the United States is likely to increase in relative terms, as Africa’s population grows faster than ours. Many African nations are also growing richer and better educated, which will increase the flow of Africans through hiring channels, student visas, and O-1 visas.

Recommended.

The post Well-planned African immigration to America will go fine appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.

item.title: Futility Closet: “We and They”
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/13/we-and-they/

Father, Mother, and Me, Sister and Auntie say All the people like us are We, And every one else is They. And They live over the sea, While We live over the way, But — would you believe it? — They look upon We As only a sort of They!

We eat pork and beef With cow-horn-handled knives. They who gobble Their rice off a leaf, Are horrified out of Their lives; And They who live up a tree, And feast on grubs and clay, (Isn’t it scandalous?) look upon We As a simply disgusting They!

We shoot birds with a gun. They stick lions with spears. Their full-dress is un-. We dress up to Our ears. They like Their friends for tea. We like Our friends to stay; And, after all that, They look upon We As an utterly ignorant They!

We eat kitcheny food. We have doors that latch. They drink milk or blood, Under an open thatch. We have Doctors to fee. They have Wizards to pay. And (impudent heathen!) They look upon We As a quite impossible They!

All good people agree, And all good people say, All nice people, like Us, are We And every one else is They: But if you cross over the sea, Instead of over the way, You may end by (think of it!) looking on We As only a sort of They!

— Kipling

item.title: Futility Closet: An Orderly Vacation
item.description:
Original article: https://www.futilitycloset.com/2026/10/13/an-orderly-vacation/

A puzzle from Peter Winkler’s excellent Mathematical Puzzles (2021):

A certain island contains a network of roads. Each road segment (between one intersection and the next) has its own name. If d is the average number of road segments that meet at an intersection, show that it’s possible to take a drive on the island that traverses at least d road segments and hits them in alphabetical order.

Each road has two ends, so the total number of road ends observed at the island’s intersections is twice the number of roads on the island. The number we’re calling d, the average number of road segments that meet at an intersection, is thus 2 m / n, where m is the number of roads on the island and n is the number of intersections.

Station a pedestrian at each intersection. At time 1, let the pedestrians at either end of the alphabetically first road traverse it, changing places. At time 2, let the pedestrians who find themselves at either end of the alphabetically second road do the same. Continue this procedure until it’s been applied to all the roads. At the end of this exercise each pedestrian will have followed an alphabetical path (because we addressed the roads in alphabetical order). Each road is traversed twice, and the number of pedestrians equals the number of intersections on the island. So the average number of roads that each pedestrian traverses is 2 m / n = d.
